The house resumed, from Thursday, March 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mrs. Fairclough.
Mr. Speaker, at long last the government is permitting the house to resume the debate on this unemployment question.
Order.

I suggest that the manner in which this debate has been delayed by the government is indicative of the attitude of the government to the problem. It would appear that they were hoping that by prolonging this debate, by stretching it out over a long period of time, it might decrease the amount of interest among members and might tend to minimize the importance of the unemployment question.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that when we recall the events leading up to the resumption of this debate we realize that it was on February 24 that the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), moved the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the serious unemployment problem in Canada. This move followed on the heels of the last announcement that the number of unplaced applicants at employment offices throughout Canada as of January 20 stood at 569,000.
When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar moved the adjournment of the house, the house leader was able to persuade him to defer the debate on unemployment until the following Monday when we were promised a supply motion. On that distinct understanding, and on the presumption that on

the following Monday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would be permitted to proceed with the matter he had initiated in this house, he agreed to forgo the motion at that time. Now, we know what happened when the supply motion was brought in not on Monday but on Tuesday. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was not permitted to proceed with the debate on unemployment that he had initiated.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Mr. Speaker,-
Sit down.

speechtext: The hon. member should address his remarks to the subject matter which is now offered for discussion. In reviewing in the manner in which he has the other events which have happened in connection with either the motion under standing order 31 moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar or the beginning of the proceedings on this particular motion to go into supply, the hon. member is somewhat reflecting upon the proceedings of this house. Mr. Speaker, my references thus far were made in an effort to indicate what

I believe is the attitude of mind toward the problem under discussion, namely, unemployment. However, in deference to your advice I am not going to pursue this particular matter; but I do want to suggest the fact that hon. members of the opposition were prepared to forgo a private members' day in order to permit this matter-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the hon. member says that the opposition was prepared to forgo a private members' day, surely he is aware of the fact that the private members' days were forgone because of unanimous consent. At this moment when he talks about the attitude of one or the other of the parties with respect to a decision that was made a few days ago he is reflecting upon the proceedings of the house. If he looks at standing order 41 he will see that he is not entitled to do that.

Mr. Speaker, there is one matter with which I feel I can deal without running foul of the rules of the house. When an announcement was made of a conference between the representatives of the provinces and the federal government, I am certain that all hon. members took it for granted that unemployment would be the first item on the agenda of any such conference. We were therefore quite amazed when the Prime Minister was questioned in this connection on March 10 and was asked whether or not unemployment would be on the agenda of that conference. It will be recalled that the Prime Minister answered in this way, as reported at page 1879 of Hansard. He said:
Mr. Speaker. I should be greatly surprised if that question was not discussed while they are here.
That was the answer to the question as to whether or not unemployment will be placed on the agenda of that conference. The Prime Minister told us that he would be surprised. He did not tell us that it is to be on the agenda. He told us he would be surprised if it is not dealt with. I am quite certain it is going to be discussed; but I suggest it will not be discussed because the federal government wants it discussed. It will be dealt with because there are premiers from some of the provinces of Canada who will come down here determined to discuss unemployment as the foremost of all problems.
When the Prime Minister was taken to task on this matter he went a little farther. He said:
.. .this is not something that can be dealt with and decided separately from the general problem

Unemployment
of the fiscal relations between the federal government and the governments of the provinces. It is an important factor in those fiscal relations and will certainly have to be considered as such.
Here again we have not a statement, not a commitment, that unemployment will receive top priority in the deliberations of that conference but just a weak sort of assurance that since unemployment does enter into the question of fiscal relations between the provincial and federal governments it unquestionably will be discussed.
I am certain that hon. members were anxious that the government should make its position quite clear that this would be taken up at the forthcoming conference the latter part of April in order to get to the heart of this unemployment problem in so far as co-operation between the provinces and the federal government is possible. I suggest that here is convincing proof of the refusal of the government to face up to the importance of unemployment in this country. The very fact that they have an important conference coming up and that they are prepared to discuss unemployment only as it relates to other matters to be discussed at that conference indicates this.
May I suggest that even if there was not a single unemployed man or woman in Canada there would still be a need for that conference and there would still be discussion about fiscal matters. To argue that we can take care of unemployment matters by any such incidental method is an affront to those who are looking for some leadership from the government at this time.
I submit that this problem of unemployment is a growing one and that procrastination on the part of the government is not going to bring about any improvement; all it will do is lead to very serious difficulties later on. The question of post-war unemployment is one that should have been given attention by this government a number of years ago. They should have acted to maintain full employment in the years immediately following the war; certainly in the last four years when they have seen a steady growth of unemployment they should have taken action. However, we have gone along the path each year seeing increasing unemployment but even if the government has failed to act in the past, the time to act is now instead of waiting until the situation becomes even more serious.
I would remind hon. members that the unemployment figure of 294,000 in 1951 has now risen to 569,000. We must remember that not all persons out of work at any given

time are registered at the national employment offices. One must also consider that before the end of winter this figure might well exceed 600,000.
The attitude of the government toward this unemployment question for many years has been merely to refuse to admit that the problem exists. They have adopted an ostrich-like attitude that if you deny the existence of the problem you will be spared the necessity of having to bring forth some solution. We have had at this session a sort of reluctant admission on the part of the government that unemployment is causing them some concern; but if the government is concerned its concern is manifested, not in positive action to solve unemployment but in making excuses and providing alibis for the past and present lack of action.
There are many excuses offered by the government for the present rate of unemployment. We are told that unemployment is frictional in character, that it is caused by seasonal or regional factors. We have always had seasonal and regional unemployment in Canada and the shameful thing is that year after year the government has taken that situation for granted and has never at any time put forth any effort toward the alleviation of the distress which occurs year in and year out owing to the regional and seasonal characteristics of our economy.
I would submit that most of these frictional causes might be examined. I would suggest that in a private enterprise economy full employment in peacetime is the exception rather than the norm. The only time that we have ever attained full employment in Canada has been during periods of war. During the latter few years of world war II we perhaps approached the closest to full employment we have ever been, and at no given time were there under 60,000 to 70,000 unplaced applicants in the employment offices. That figure, which represented about 2 per cent of the labour force, indicates perhaps the actual amount of unemployment which might be attributed to frictional causes. Translated into the terms of our present-day population and using that 2 per cent figure, my suggestion is that any unemployment in excess of 2 per cent of our labour force is cyclical or general unemployment, and that if the government chooses to argue that unemployment is due to frictional causes their argument is valid to an extent of not more than 2 per cent of the labour force.
If the government argues on that basis they could still not account for the fact that in excess of this 2 per cent we have around

half a million Canadians who are presently out of work and who have no immediate prospects of employment. My group have always suggested that we cannot look upon seasonal or regional unemployment as a normal thing. We have always maintained that the government should have planned to make provision for this yearly recurring problem in this country. This government through a public investment program should have created employment opportunities in those parts of Canada which are most seriously affected by regional unemployment and should have provided supplementary employment opportunities for those Canadians who must make their living on a seasonal basis.
When we consider the difficult times through which these people go who are unemployed annually for a period of time, we should also consider the tremendous wastage in manpower. The champions of private enterprise are always prone to point out the number of man-hours lost through labour disturbances, strikes and lockouts, but they never seem to pay much attention to the tremendous wastage of manpower due to unemployment. I suggest that this problem of seasonal and regional unemployment should have been faced by the government a long time ago, and their failure to deal with this problem now means that the unemployment problem they are faced with is a problem of cyclical unemployment.
I think the statistics bear out the facts of this situation. We know that during the years 1952 to 1954 the labour force of this country increased by some 122,000, yet during that time jobs did not keep pace. It is quite obvious that an increase in the labour force must be accompanied by a proportionate increase in the number of new jobs created if unemployment is not to increase. This places a responsibility upon the government because the government is the only agency in Canada which is in a position to do anything about it.
As compared to the increase in the labour force of 122,000 during the years 1952 to 1954 to which I referred, there was an increase of just over 73,000 in new jobs created through public and private investment. Not only did we fail to make a dent in the existing unemployment during those years, but in each year there was a net increase in the number of unemployed. It seems obvious that employment opportunities will have to be made for this net increase in addition to providing employment for those who are presently on the rolls of the unemployed.
If this is not done by private capital investment then it obviously must be done by public investment. In any event there can be no
Unemployment
excuse for delaying action and allowing a great number of Canadian citizens to go without jobs and remain in want. In addition to the increase in our labour force there is also the question of increased productivity of labour to be considered. The increased rate of capital investment in the post-war years is now paying off industry in increased labour productivity.
We know that important technological processes and new industrial techniques mean that fewer men are required to turn out the same amount of goods.
An official of the steel workers' union pointed out at a meeting held a few days ago that steel production in the United States this year would be about the same as last year but this year the steel companies will require 100,000 fewer workers to do the same amount of work.
This is a change which should bring about great benefits to the country as a whole. To the workers it should mean fewer hours of work and better wages. To the consumers it should mean lower prices. To the nation as a whole it should mean that the benefits obtained through these savings should be made available in investment programs to expand our economy. But what has happened? We find that instead of these benefits being apportioned throughout the country as a whole the benefits are going to the owners of capital and in many cases men are being dropped from the employment rolls and are now swelling the ranks of the unemployed.
It appears quite obvious this problem cannot be left to private business because private business economists have never in the past been able to correct the situation. This is simply due to the fact that a correction of the situation would involve a change in the system and they are not prepared to admit a change is necessary.
The hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Reinke), speaking in this debate, pointed that out quite clearly when he reminded the members on the government side of the house, and he might have reminded the hon. members on my right or my left as well, that they are believers in free enterprise and as such unemployment is one of those things which occur in the normal business cycle. Any college freshman taking an elementary course in economics is taught that under the free enterprise system you have a period of prosperity followed by a downward trend known as a recession. Then a depression occurs which is followed by a period known as a recovery and this is followed by another short period of prosperity which invariably occurs in wartime. The student is taught that this process repeats itself throughout history.

Unemployment
Under these circumstances, if we are going to tackle this problem intelligently we are going to have to think in terms of fundamentals. There is no comfort for the unemployed in this country in knowing that an argument is taking place between the government and the opposition as to how many unemployed there are in Canada. I am quite sure that if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is able to convince the opposition that there are a few thousand less unemployed than the opposition claims, it is going to be of little or no comfort to those Canadians who are without jobs.
I suggest we have to get down to the root causes of the problem if we hope to accomplish anything as a result of this debate.
The group I represent maintains that full employment is the answer. We insist that nothing short of full employment will meet the needs and the legitimate requirements of the Canadian people.
In case any hon. members are in doubt as to the meaning of the term "full employment" I am going to quote, by way of explanation, not from a socialist economist but from a statement made by the man who is possibly the person most directly connected with this concept, Sir William Beveridge. He sums up full employment in these words:
More vacant jobs than unemployed men. not slightly fewer jobs. It means that jobs are at fair wages, of such a kind and so located that the unemployed man can reasonably be expected to take them; it means, by consequence, that the normal lag between losing one job and finding another will be very short.
We maintain that full employment should be the goal of this government and that the Canadian people will be satisfied with nothing less.
One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker. Full employment will not be brought about without economic planning by the government.
Hon. members in this debate have stated that we should give assistance to private enterprise. They say the government should give handouts to private concerns in the hope that they will provide employment opportunities. It is the old story: when business is good and profits are rolling in, the government is told to keep its hands off private enterprise; but in difficult times private enterprise is the first to come running to the government asking for assistance of some sort.
I suggest that if private enterprise is going to reap the benefits and profits which come with prosperous times they must be prepared to accept the bad along with the good. I also believe if the government is going to be called upon to spend any money the money should be spent by the government in the interests of the people of this country.

I would like to remind the hon. members of this house that three of four groups in this house are by their own admission champions of the economic system which insists upon leaving to private business the conduct and control of the economic affairs of this country. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that many hon. members of all parties understand the real cause of unemployment in this country that when we suggest a fundamental reform is necessary we are not suggesting anything which was not suggested many years ago by leaders of both the Liberal and Conservative parties.
Mr. Bennett, in January 1935, a week before the opening of the House of Commons, went on the air and announced his new deal. At that time he indicated that he understood the nature of the existing economic system when he spoke of "soulless corporations," and "corporations whose bankrolls loom larger than your happiness". He called for widespread changes in the economic system. His statements were apparently so radical that they offended and frightened his more affluent supporters and they deserted him and put their financial backing behind the Liberal party which soundly defeated his government at the polls a few months later.
The late W. L. Mackenzie King did not criticize Bennett because his program was radical. Indeed, he said that the trouble with the program was that it did not go far enough and did not reach the heart of the matter. In the debates of 1935 we find the following statement by the late W. L. Mackenzie King. I remind you that these are not the words of J. S. Woodsworth. These are the words of the late Mr. King, recorded in Hansard of January 21, 1935, at page 35:
You may have democracy in government combined with democracy in industry. You cannot have democracy in government combined with autocracy in industry. The latter two are as ill mated as the former are congenial. And as long as the capitalist system remains ... a system whereby industrial policies will be exclusively controlled by capitalist investors, parliament intervening here and there to correct incidental evils only, just so long you will have no reform that is fundamental or far-reaching.
On the same day Mr. King also said:
No changes in the capitalist system which keep the capital investor secure in his position as the controller of industrial policy will ever in this world bring about any reform worthy of the name.
It is quite evident, Mr. Speaker, that during the thirties both the leader of the Conservative party of that day and the leader of the Liberal party understood the true nature of the crisis of the time, but they gave lip service only and clung to the economic system which would not permit of a change.

This brings me back to the main theme of my remarks this afternoon. If we are going to face up to the unemployment situation in Canada we must recognize the real causes of unemployment. I may say that apparently not all hon. members in this house are in support of full employment. I recall not many years ago the premier of Alberta visited Ottawa and said that the attainment of full employment in peacetime is as antiquated as an old maid's dream and as improbable of attainment. A few years later the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) said any time the government sets out as its major conscious objective full employment, social security and economic planning, then that government is leading the people down the road to slavery. The hon. member says, "Right." Well, he should see the cleavage and the division there. If we want to bring about a situation of full employment we have to recognize that it involves planning by the government. The government is a democratic institution which represents the people of Canada. The main issue is not a question of whether or not we are going to have control and direction of our economic system. The control and direction of our economic system already exists. The question is whether those controls are going to be exercised by big business in this country in their own interests or whether those controls are going to be exercised by a democratic parliament in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole. That is the main issue.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of other causes of unemployment which have been dealt with by some other hon. members. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) pointed out the other day or offered as an excuse the statement that the unemployment situation is as good today as it was last year. I think those are his exact words. He suggested that productive activity has not been sufficient to absorb the net increase in persons coming into the labour force. He suggested the problem. I now suggest that the government tell us what they are going to do about that problem. Are they just going to continue to see this trend continue each year where our unemployment situation is going to get progressively worse, or what measures are they going to undertake to see to it that there is sufficient investment-and I am afraid that of necessity it will have to be public investment-to take care of the increase in our labour force?
There are several other factors entering into our unemployment problem in this country. Our export markets and the increase in private investment capital have always been important factors in the employment picture
Unemployment
in this country. I am not going to say anything about our deteriorating trade position. That matter has been dealt with by some other hon. members on other occasions. However, I want to point out that this last year was the first year since the war in which private capital investment in this country dropped off. In each year since the war there had been an increase in private capital investment. Last year that dropped. Actually the amount is not too great, but when we consider that the population of this country has been growing and that the labour force has been increasing, a fall in the private investment capital in this country can mean only one thing, namely continued and growing unemployment.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a debate of this kind, if it is going to be more than an academic discussion of a vital economic problem, must take into account the political realities of the day. When we come to discuss unemployment, I hope hon. members in other groups, when they rise in this house to discuss this problem, will tell us just how they propose to go about bringing about full employment without government planning, or how they propose to undertake the necessary measures to alleviate the distress in this country without placing the responsibility where it must inevitably rest, namely on the shoulders of the government.
I am not going to deal with the question, Mr. Speaker, of the record of the Liberals and the Conservatives in the past. On a former occasion I had something to say about unemployment and some hon. member across the way said, "Why do you not deal with Social Credit?" I did not do so at that time because, as I suggested, that group, of their own volition, have placed themselves squarely in the forefront of the struggle to maintain the special privileges of private enterprise in this country. I think that the quotations I gave a short while ago indicate their thinking to some extent. I do not think I have ever heard any more conservative or reactionary point of view put forth anywhere in the house than that which has been put forward by the members to my left on this question of full employment.
There was a time, Mr. Speaker, when the people might have had some doubt as to where these people stood. I can recall, when I was a high school student, going out to hear the late William Aberhart. After entering the meeting I was afraid that I had got into a communist meeting by mistake because of the way he ran down the banks. Talk about radicalism! All the other groups in this country were moderate compared with the forerunners of the present group in parliament. But what is the situation today? We find that a few years ago in the Alberta

Unemployment
legislature the minister of mines admitted that while the government of that province had made $89-9 million out of oil, one man, a corporation lawyer in the city of Calgary who at that time was holidaying on a rented yacht in Bermuda, had made $90 million. In other words, one man had made more money out of Alberta oil at that time than had all the people of Alberta put together. Yet we are told that the natural resources belong to the people.
Let us now look at the amazing situation in the province of British Columbia. Here is a situation involving a political party which damned the banks a short while ago. They used to put posters out on the telephone poles saying: Tax the banks; it does not cost them anything. It was not many years ago that court cases were taken against some pamphleteers in the city of Edmonton for talking about bankers' toadies. What is the amazing situation today? We find that the former minister of finance in a Social Credit government and now financial adviser to that government has been appointed to the board of directors of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I think an extremely interesting comment was made by a writer in the Financial Post on March 5. In discussing this matter he says in part as follows:
These debating points must amuse Premier Bennett, for they divert public attention from his master plan. That plan is nothing less than the liquidation of his old Conservative party, the seizure of the political Right in Canada-
With a capital "R" for right, of course.
-and the capture of parliament under a thin Social Credit label. To him and other former Conservatives around him, Victoria is only a whistle stop on the main line to Ottawa.
For these purposes, suitable obeisances are made to Major Douglas, the A plus B theorem and the original bag of tricks but Social Credit must be made to look safe, respectable and orthodox to the Canadian voter.
What could be better proof of safety, respectability and orthodoxy than the welcome of Mr. Gunderson, financial director of a Social Credit government, into the directorate of a great private bank? What more reassuring than Mr. Gunderson's belated discovery that private banks are immaculate under the new interpretation of Social Credit when they were a combination of Judas Iscariot and Jack the Ripper under the old interpretation?
It seems to me that someone is pulling the wool over someone's eyes. Either Mr. Gunderson is pulling the wool over the eyes of the people who, over the years, have supported the theories of Major Douglas, or he is pulling the wool over the eyes of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. For my money, Mr. Speaker, I am quite satisfied that neither the Canadian Bank of Commerce nor any of our
[Mr. Ellis. 1
other chartered banks is going to appoint to their board of directors a man who believes in the A plus B theorem.
Then, to bring the picture up to date, one need only look at the feverish attempts on the part of this group to find a leader somewhere in the province of Saskatchewan. They have an organization. They had a convention. They had a properly elected executive. But apparently outsiders had come into that province. These faithful, loyal Social Crediters are being stabbed in the back in the interests of the present British Columbia leadership who are contributing to the sabotage of the existing organization in the interests of those outside the province.
Oh, oh.
I know you cannot take it. I realize that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I am not going to discuss further this inner struggle between the two wings of the Tory party but I am going to suggest that, in our own province, the men and women who over the years have announced some faith and some support of these ideologies, fallacious though they may be, are nevertheless quite perturbed about not just interference but outright control from outside the province. I am quite certain that the people of Saskatchewan are as good as people elsewhere in Canada. I know that our Liberals are just as good as the Liberals of Ontario, and I am quite sure that our Social Crediters are just as good as the Social Crediters in British Columbia and Alberta. I suggest that our own people are well able to look after their own internal political organization.
I want to make this one observation. Often I find it difficult to distinguish between the three parties I have mentioned several times this afternoon, Conservative, Liberal and Social Credit, but there is one thing that I think must be said in fairness to the Liberals and Conservatives. Irrespective of their adherence to an economic philosophy, at least they do have conventions at which they elect their leaders in a democratic fashion. I must give credit to both the old established parties for that.
Different from the C.C.F.
Returning to the motion-
Hear, hear.

-our main concern is what action the government is going to take at this time to meet the unemployment problem. I suggest

they can start first by assuring the people of Canada that they are prepared to honour the commitment they made in 1945 to take care of the employable unemployed. They can provide the necessary financial assistance to take care of those who are without jobs at the present time until such time as employment opportunities are provided for these people. They can also increase transfer payments to provide a higher level of purchasing power throughout the country. Through a properly planned public investment program they can develop our natural resources to expand the economy of the country and at the same time provide needed employment opportunities to the people.
Who in this house today, Mr. Speaker, can argue that there is not work to be done? When we consider the great need for new homes, the great need for schools, hospitals, highways, irrigation projects, railway grade crossing protection and the host of other much needed works, there is no excuse whatsoever for any government in Canada not taking action at the present time. I suggest, for example, that the government might begin on some of those projects that have been under active consideration for some considerable time.
Coming from the province of Saskatchewan, I suggest that the federal government should accept the generous offer of financial assistance by the provincial government and start work immediately on the South Saskatchewan river dam. We know that at the present time the unemployment problem has spread throughout the length and breadth of the country. There is not a province in Canada where there is not needed work to be done. As a specific example I repeat my suggestion that the government should announce at this time that it is prepared to go ahead with the immediate construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
There is a need in this country for work to be done. We have natural resources in abundance. What is more, we have capable people who are willing and anxious to work. What is the government waiting for? We have all the requirements necessary to put our people to work. All that is required is intelligent leadership on the part of the government. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)-and reference has been made to this before-when he spoke to the New Reform club in Quebec on September 19 last told his hearers, and of course the country, that it was the government's job to find work for all. We agree. He said if the government was not smart enough to organize our economy to provide work for all it was incompetent. We agree.
Unemployment
If the members who support the government take the Prime Minister at his word, if they actually believe that the government has provided jobs for all, then I suggest they should go to the people of the country and explain away the over half million unemployed we have at the present time. If the government supporters admit, as they must, that the government has not provided jobs for all, then I also suggest that they take the Prime Minister at his word and vote nonconfidence in the government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: For a small part of the hon. member's speech I think he may have been slightly out of order. If that is so, I should like to ask hon. members not to take me to task because I did not do anything about it. It struck me that the hon. member was perhaps taking a tangent away from unemployment when he spoke about the method of selecting leaders among the various parties. Maybe he took advantage of the fact that for a while several of our colleagues came to the chair to speak to me. I hope that the fact I was not attentive at that particular moment is not going to be held against me and that the debate will not be too much out of order from now on, because I intend to listen.

Mr. Speaker, after your warning words I am rather circumscribed as to some of the things I might have said in answer to the hon. member who has just taken his seat. However, I will be keeping entirely within the limits of the subject under discussion if I suggest to my hon. friend that, in view of the fact there is a nursery of socialism in the province of Saskatchewan, it might be well for the hon. gentleman and those associated with him to apply the biblical injunction-physician, heal thyself. Unemployment in the province of Saskatchewan is in my opinion-and I have statistics here to bear it out-larger in proportion to population than in any other province in the Dominion of Canada. I have the records week by week of unemployment in Prince Albert, Moose Jaw, Regina, Saskatoon and Yorkton. These records extend from the 28th of January to the 18th of February.
These records indicate an increase in unemployment week by week in my own province which reveals a serious situation. During the weeks to which I have made reference there was an increase in unemployment of 26 per cent to 46 per cent over a year ago. In one case, the city of Regina, during a period of three weeks the increase is some 55 per cent. While I am in no way absolving and do not intend to absolve the government of the country for

Unemployment
its failure to act, I suggest to my hon. friend that, with the resources available in Saskatchewan, it strikes me as passing strange that the government of that province has not seen fit to do what the Frost government has done in Ontario-
Call an election.

My hon. friend says, "call an election". I am dealing at the moment with unemployment, but I shall return to that. The Frost government has brought into effect in Ontario a program of public works similar to though greater than that introduced in the legislature of Quebec in the month of November. While these other provinces, tired of waiting for the federal government to act, have acted, the government of Saskatchewan has sat in idleness in the face of the rising unemployment problem. I listened to the hon. member talk about private enterprise. I ask him: What has happened in Saskatchewan with respect to the public enterprises operated in that province? Have they thought of the employed? Go to the city of Prince Albert. What about the famous box factory there? Last September and October the employees of that government institution were told, "We are not making a profit, so out you go."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon.
member at this point, because if he continues to criticize the provincial government of Saskatchewan he may prompt other members to come to the defence of the government of Saskatchewan and we will be discussing, during this debate on unemployment, provincial actions with respect to some problems. Inasmuch as the unemployment situation may be affected I think there might be some passing references to provincial action, but we must remain within the sphere of federal jurisdiction. I do not think we should undertake a debate on the merits or demerits of the various policies adopted from time to time by provincial governments.

I listened for 25 minutes to the excoriation of private enterprise. I was simply pointing out to my hon. friend, who says socialism is the answer, that it certainly has not been in Saskatchewan where several of the government businesses have had to close down because of the tremendous deficits which they suffered. I will say no more than that out of deference to Your Honour. I would have liked to place these things on the record before the house, so that my hon. friend speaking in theories might be answered by the experience of the party in power in Saskatchewan of which he speaks in such adulatory and eulogistic tones with regard to what it has done. Yet,

whenever there has not been a profit they have put the employees out to join the unemployed and go on unemployment insurance. Further than that I shall not go at the present time because of what Your Honour has said.
Now, sir, the resolution that is before the house was moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). It reads as follows, as recorded at page 1606 of Hansard for March 1, 1955:
in the opinion of this house, because of the grave state of unemployment in Canada as disclosed by the joint statement of the Department of Labour-
And so on. Then, it continues:
-the government should immediately give consideration to the formulation of plans to deal with this emergency, and to the necessary steps to establish a long-term program for expanding employment to be presented to parliament during the present session.
It seems a long while ago, sir, that this debate started. So far as I am concerned, I sat here and listened to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). The debate started with two sets of figures as to the degree of unemployment. The minister finally supplied the revised version. His views, and I shall refer to them in a moment, were that conditions are not cheerful; not altogether black; the government is concerned; unemployment is not too serious. Then, a few minutes later he mentioned the reasonably good showing in 1954, and that it should not be forgotten. In another part of his speech he said men who are able to work but are without jobs, and who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits, exist in far too great numbers.
Well, what have the unemployed to hope for from the debate that has taken place? What has the government to offer? What salutary degree of hope and expectation may rise in the hearts of the unemployed of this country as they listened to the minister's lengthy speech in which he pointed out that conditions were not good, but they were good in one place. He said that we could easily have more unemployment and greater employment at the same time. In another place he said that the unemployment situation may appear a good deal worse than last year, and it may lead one to conclude that both the economic situation and the employment picture are deteriorating.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said he very seriously regretted the developing unemployment across the country when he spoke in the house some weeks ago. On another occasion he said, very seriously, that the government regrets the developing

unemployment. But what, sir, has been said by the government? Today I think the hothouse development of expanding production through defence has placed the government in a position where they are unable to even suggest that something be done about this problem. They express solicitude. They mobilize statistics. But the Prime Minister, from whom the people of Canada want to hear, with the prestige of his position, remains silent in the face of a problem that wrings the hearts of the people.
The government has been asked by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) to do something. The same request has been made by hon. members on this side of the house, yet there has been no word of hope. In so far as unemployment is concerned the government has been as idle as a painted ship upon a painted ocean. The Minister of Labour mentioned how good conditions were six months ago. This reminded me of an old story on the prairies. A man had died in a blizzard and sympathy was given to the mourners by saying, "Just remember, six months ago yesterday was the hottest day of the year." What a hopeless picture! The government, faced for the first time with serious unemployment that has been mounting over the years, is unable to give any hope. We are unable to rouse them into placing before the people of Canada some of the picture.
Mention was made of the fact that Mr. Bennett came into power in August, 1930, after unemployment had been mounting at a terrific rate following the stock market break in 1929. In the speech from the throne in 1930, we find these words; that were placed in the mouth of the governor general:
It affords me much pleasure to greet you at the commencement of another session of parliament, and to be able to congratulate you upon the continued prosperity of the country. The year 1929 was the most productive year in the history of Canada. In industries, other than agriculture, employment reached the highest point on record: new construction was the largest known. Mining production was of unequalled value. Manufacturing production surpassed all previous records. There was vast increase in the development of hydroelectric power. The products of our fields and our herds reached higher standards of excellence and quality than at any previous time. The dominion is already recovering from the seasonal slackness evident at the end of the year, and it is not to be forgotten that the bulk of the 1929 wheat crop still remains in Canadian hands for final disposition.
Sir, that was the picture in February of 1930. No one here wants to speak of depression. We on this side of the house hope that the government will act because there is no depression in other countries of the world. In Britain there is no such thing as serious unemployment today, the unemployment in
Unemployment
Britain being less than half of our unemployment with a population several times greater than ours. The same condition prevails in West Germany and in other private enterprise countries. For instance, the other day the Prime Minister of Australia said that in the face of one million immigrants who have gone into Australia in the last few years, he would welcome Canadians.
We do not believe in preaching pessimism; we do not want to see the condition of affairs brought about which will create panic; but we are asking the government to act now as they were asked to act in 1930. If hon. members will read that speech alongside the speech placed in the mouth of the Governor General this year they will see the similarity. Sir, this is not something new that has come to the attention of the government. It has been mounting for the last several years. The Leader of the Opposition over and over again has pointed out that we are pricing ourselves out of world markets. He pointed out the danger to our economic system of the acceleration of the trend toward increasing unemployment.
In 1954 the revenues of the Canadian National Railways were down by some $60 million as compared with 1953, and the Canadian Pacific revenues were down some $50 million. I mention at this time that we have been trying for days to find out what is the degree of layoffs on the Canadian National Railways. That information is denied us. We have got as far as to find out that some 3,500 were laid off between December and January. Why not face that picture? Is it not a fact that some 10,000 have been laid off? The railwaymen ask: what is the picture for the future? After all, it is a government corporation and they have a right to expect information regarding the railway company owned by the dominion.
What about trade conditions and agriculture? So far as agriculture is concerned, no matter what statistics may be mobilized by the government, there is a continuing reduction in purchasing power, there is a continuing reduction in the income of the farmer and an increase in the cost of the things that the farmer has to buy. When we think of the initial price of wheat at $1.40 a bushel we go back to 1935-39 and we find that today wheat has a purchasing power of 53| cents a bushel.
What about our trade with the United States? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said the other day that we are doing something to prevent their closing out their markets to us. We do not know what has been done. Certainly, whatever has been done other than the writing of two notes and

Unemployment
a visit to Washington has not brought about any change. What is our situation in the United States? In January, 1954, we imported from the United States $202 million worth of goods; in January of this year we imported $208 million worth. Our exports in the same period increased from $160 million to $183 million. In other words, the spread of imports into Canada is increasing at the expense of the exports. By our exports to the United States we continue to export employment to that country by shipping them tens of millions of dollars' worth of raw products or partly manufactured products and exhaustible resources that can never be restored in this country. In the face of that, and our importations of manufactured goods, the situation is continuing to become worse day by day and week by week. While we raise this matter, and have raised it for several years, the answer of the government is, in effect, we hope for the best. Now we have a serious unemployment situation and I am going to ask the Prime Minister a few questions that have to be answered. They cannot be avoided. They are questions that every municipality is asking today.
The municipalities are loaded down with unemployment relief. The residents of our urban communities cannot bear it any longer. What is to be done about the unemployed employables? What is the attitude of the government? Well, if I understand the press of this country, almost without exception the press says that constitutional matters are today being raised as a smokescreen to relieve this government of its responsibilities. You cannot feed 550,000 hungry stomachs by promising them that if the constitution permitted it something would be done. The government adopts that attitude. Who is responsible? In the 1920's we thought that the constitutional argument was sufficient. Over and over again Mr. Mackenzie King said that nothing could be done, and finally, when unemployment had risen to unheard of levels, the government went out of office. I do not say that the Bennett government did everything that should have been done. They faced a situation where there was depression everywhere in the world, where the situation was the same in every free enterprise and socialist country, where farm prices had fallen to unheard of levels everywhere in the world; but at least the government of Mr. Bennett said: we will give grants in order to relieve municipalities of the load of responsibility and also to assist the province. An amendment to the constitution was brought in with a great blare. Tremendous changes were being effected in 1941 or 1942.
[Mr. Dielenbaker.l
As a result of that amendment the Unemployment Insurance Act was placed on the statute books. I am asking the Prime Minister, and I think the country has a right to an answer: Does he accept the proposals of the government of Canada of August, 1945, made to the conference of that year? These are the representations made by the government of Canada of which he was then a member and of which the Minister of Agriculture was also a member. The proposals placed before that conference were as follows. I am quoting from page 42 of the proposals of the government of Canada:
Over the past 7 or 8 years there have been recommendations by the national employment commission, the Sirois commission and others, that the dominion should assume responsibility tor necessary relief to the employable unemployed. It has been generally suggested that the dominion should accept this obligation as part of any general settlement with the provinces.
After discussing the matter the government went on to propose:
As a part of the general arrangement with the provincial governments, the dominion government now proposes to establish a practicable and comprehensive system of assistance to ablebodied unemployed persons as soon as possible, rather than waiting until the need for it actually arises. It is thought necessary not to permit the recurrence of the problems of administration being separated from financial responsibility . . .
Then it says:
The dominion is therefore accompanying its proposal for general acceptance of responsibility with a concrete plan for its implementation in the field of assistance for employable unemployed persons.
And so it goes. The plan proposes acceptance of dominion responsibility for employable unemployed persons and provincial and local responsibility for unemployables. I ask the Prime Minister: Are you running away from that offer? Are you prepared to stand by that offer? If you are, when this preliminary conference takes place in April, there is nothing to stop you from placing this matter in the 1945 form before this conference to the end that action will be taken, late but not too late as compared with what the situation will be if the unemployed have to wait until fall. If there is anyone who wants to suggest that I have omitted any material part of that, let him say so. I have read every line of it. There is no excuse today for the government to hide behind a subterfuge as they are doing on this occasion.
What is going to happen at this conference in April? The premiers are coming and are going to decide what they will do when they start to do something. Why does not the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gather together his economic committee and formulate a general system to place before this meeting

in April with regard to this problem of unemployment instead of postponing and procrastinating until September, October or November and then another possible postponement of action until another conference. This government cannot escape responsibility for its failure to have acted before now. Speaking in Quebec last September the Prime Minister used these words:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent.
That is what one Canadian Press dispatch said. Another report placed an "s" on the "incompetent" and you can have it either way. That is what the Prime Minister said last September. Then the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) spoke to the congress of labour, and I quote the following from the report of that meeting:
Hon. Milton Gregg. Minister of Labour, cautiously predicted the coming year would see some improvement in the employment picture. "It is difficult to foretell long-range future developments, but there appears to be no real reason for being gloomy," Mr. Gregg declared.
Then we have the speech from the throne, that delightful document, which stated that unemployment is regional and seasonal. That is really reminiscent of the February 1930 speech from the throne. Then the Financial Post reported on unemployment and quoted one of these sources which are always anonymous; high in anonymity and low in permission for their names to be used. This was in January and this anonymous person is reported as saying that he believed that unemployment would fall behind last year's figure.
What about British Columbia? The government of British Columbia got in touch with this government and pointed out the situation which was created by people coming to that province because of the salubrious climate that exists there. In answer to a request for assistance, and referring to the post-war period, the Prime Minister said that he believed that the greatly improved economic conditions since that time and the additional fact that unemployment insurance, family allowance, old age security and other welfare payments, which cost the federal government about $1 billion annually, had reduced the cost of unemployment to a level within the financial capacity of the province.
I submit with great respect that that statement does not take into consideration that today the federal government is collecting almost 78 per cent of the revenues of this country. There has been a refusal to do anything in recent weeks. As soon as this debate got under way the Bank of Canada 50433-129
Unemployment
issued one of its optimistic statements and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) put out his booklet on private and public investment. Those things are not enough. The government does not even recognize that there is serious unemployment. Unless they do recognize that fact they cannot achieve in their minds any actuality of a solution for the problem. I was reading Edmund Burke the other night and I saw something that is quite fitting. He said:
We can never walk surely but by being sensible of our blindness.
How applicable that is to this government which is so insensible to its blindness, to its own postponing and procrastinating. It is ready to promise action some time in the future. The Prime Minister was asked by an hon. member from Toronto whether this matter of unemployment would be brought before this meeting of the provincial premiers in April and he refused categorically to say that that would be done and that action would be taken.
That is the position of affairs here in Canada, which is an island of unemployment, as it were, in the midst of other private enterprise countries which are going ahead and which have kept unemployment down to basic levels. Surely that fact alone and the loss of our trade from month to month and from year to year, accelerating as it has in the last few years, should cause this government to decide to lift itself from its supine attitude, not of indifference but of apathy coupled with hope, and actually do something to meet the situation of the unemployed who are today asking parliament to act. The municipalities are saying that they cannot continue to carry the load they are carrying today.
You say to me: What suggestions have the opposition to offer? I repeat that we do not believe that inaction should be allowed to continue. We believe that the Prime Minister spoke words of deep and abiding wisdom last September. All we ask is that those words of wisdom be translated into action, for the fact is that nothing effective is being done.
As to our suggestions, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) suggested that there should be a dominion-provincial conference on unemployment. Why could it not be held? Why could not this conference in April be held with reference to this matter and plans made respecting other fiscal matters? That is the first question I ask.
Next, what about a reduction in taxation? I think we are going to secure a reduction in taxation because of certain speeches that

Unemployment
have been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and also because of the suggestion the other evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there might be a deficit this year. Those two things seem to telegraph an advance notice of a reduction in taxation.
As far as deficit financing is concerned, I believe that economists generally agree that it is a means of reducing unemployment and encouraging business. Seven American economists gave evidence before the United States Senate committee on the budget. Professor William Vickery of Columbia University said:
We should err, if at all. on the side of too much stimulus, too large a deficit, rather than too little.
Professor J. K. Galbraith, professor of economics at Harvard, advocated reductions in personal income tax as a means of restoring a weakened economy. I believe that there must be a reduction in taxation. Today company taxation is placing too great a load on initiative and in addition is taxing Canada out of the markets of the world.
Having said that, I should like to hear the Prime Minister, with that prestige to which I make sincere reference, say that we are going to give a lead to the people of Canada. One of the major causes of our loss of markets is the high cost of government. What have they done this year? They boast of a reduction in the cost of government. They reduced those costs by a paltry $4 million over and above the defence reduction. While we reduce by a paltry $4 million the United States, in the fiscal year ending in June last, by the application of business principles and by following the recommendations of the Hoover commission, was able to cut expenditures $6-7 billion and taxes by $7-5 billion.
I would like to hear the Prime Minister give to the people of Canada a message to the effect that as far as possible the dumping of our exhaustible and irreplaceable mineral wealth into the United States, which also means the export of employment would, as far as possible, cease. I would like to hear him say that we in Canada would follow the policy so often suggested by the financial critic of the opposition, and increase the fabrication of these raw materials in Canada. Such a move would give encouragement to Canadian producers and would ensure an expansion of jobs for the unemployed.
As an essential method of tax relief and a means of revitalizing industry there should be provision for an accelerated write-off to encourage capital expansion by industry. These are the kind of things we have been advocating for the last three or four years. The

answer in every case has been that these things are unnecessary. We are forced to conclude that this is the answer, because action has not been taken upon them.
I would like to speak about trade. If four years ago the government of this country had followed the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition, which was supported by other hon. members, and given leadership in the convening of a British commonwealth conference, it could not have been but beneficial. However, we were answered by jeers and no action was taken when we made this suggestion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is about to take a trip to Australia and New Zealand in order to discuss trade. That is all to the good. I hope, however, he is more successful in that trip than he was in the trip to South America. In the year following his South American visit I believe our trade fell by something like $50 million, although I do not attribute the result to that cause.
When the Prime Minister was asked, before departing for the prime ministers' conference, what stand he would take on the question of trade we were unable to get an answer. Since his return we are forced to conclude from his statements that little was accomplished in this regard, the reason being that international problems crowded out the consideration of matters which are particularly pertinent and appropriate to the preservation of our economic life. It must never be forgotten that Lenin predicted in 1923 that communism would never come into control until such time as the private enterprise nations engaged in a major economic conflict, the have-nots against the haves. Only then, he indicated, would there occur that breakdown in economic life under free enterprise that would permit communism to take over.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in 1945 and 1946 the government told us about a shelf of public works projects. Where is that shelf? I think you can find it filed under "E", bearing the heading "Elections". Certainly the subject of public works projects is never discussed except during election periods. It is only at election time that the shelf is pulled partly open and the hope is expressed that great public works projects will be proceeded with. At election time the old perennial, the South Saskatchewan dam, is hauled out and repolished. Where is the shelf?
It is bare.

What is being done about public works projects? What are some of the things that could be done? I know that when I mention this subject someone will refer to the constitutional division of powers. Although

constitutional difficulties in the United States so far as highways are concerned are somewhat similar to those in Canada, the President of the United States in the interests of defence and also to increase tourist traffic and facilitate transportation between states has undertaken a $100 billion project for new highways.
What about northern Canada? Today we are building radar defence stations in the north. Military authorities have told me those radar defence stations can be easily rendered inaccessible. For that reason I believe defence highways have a place in our NATO expenditures and in our continental defence program for North America. In 1919 assistance was given to the provinces. In 1912 Sir Wilfrid Laurier joined with Sir Robert Borden in supporting a similar project in order to foster development within the country.
These are a few of the matters I believe should be considered today. I ask the Prime Minister now, before taking my seat and before my time elapses, will he not arise and offer some hope to the people of Canada. Five or six hundred thousand people are asking, "What is the government going to do?" By way of reply I do not want to hear the kind of speech my gallant and hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) gave to this house, which was simply a conglomeration of incongruities. The people are asking for a promise of action. Will the Prime Minister not assure the Canadian people that he believes action is necessary and that when this conference meets in three, four or five weeks, one of the first things to which this conference will give consideration is the problem of unemployment? Will he not state that he realizes that if we continue to deliberately delude ourselves concerning the unemployment situation we shall bring about a fear complex in this country which will have serious results in the future?

Mr. Speaker, I have two reasons for taking part in this debate. The first is a statement made by the hon. member for Regina City to the effect that the government has never done anything for the unemployed. If unemployment insurance were suddenly cut off in the city of Regina he would know that something has been done. The hon. member for Prince Albert also said the government is doing nothing at this time to alleviate the unemployment situation. I would ask both hon. members to refer to a speech delivered by an hon. member on this side of the house.
Some things which have been said on this side of the house are worth repeating. Hansard of March 1, 1955 contains a statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning what has been done to assist the unemployed 50433-129J
Unemployment
in Canada. Although there is a list of the economic policies which the government has pursued I shall refer only to No. 11. He said several major projects were completed or were nearing completion, such as the great lakes waterway, the Canso causeway, and railway extensions to Lynn Lake and Kitimat. In addition the major projects initiated last year included a $30 million military camp and housing project at Gagetown, dredging at Yarmouth, and dredging in the first narrows at Vancouver. In addition the Minister of Public Works has been urging the provincial governments to get busy on the development of the trans-Canada highway. I just wonder at the imagination of hon. members who can say the government is doing nothing.
The other reason I rose is to show what Fort William is doing. I represent Fort William. I should like to quote from the Times-Journal of February 22. This Times-Journal is one of the great papers of Canada. Christmas week they published on the front page "No Bad Deeds Published on the Front Page this Week". They seek to tell the truth.
This is what Fort William had been doing prior to February 22. They organized a "do it now" campaign. I remember that during the first war there were two things of which we tried to remind ourselves at home. The first was to keep the home fires burning, and the second was that everybody should do his bit. I think doing a little bit is far better than talking a great deal. This article in connection with the "do it now" campaign is headed "Job Drive Cuts Unemployment" and reads as follows:
Proportionately, unemployment is being held down as compared with last year as a result of the "do it now" job campaign now under way in the city, G. J. Turgeon, manager of the Fort William national employment service office, reported today.
"Last year about this time, the figures were soaring," Mr. Turgeon said. "This year, the weekly figures are fairly steady. Instead of 175,200 persons reporting in each week, we are getting 35 or 40, and many are being provided with jobs in short order."
Mr. Turgeon said the campaign to get industry, merchants and householders to do all possible work now when skilled tradesmen and plenty o' '*bour is available is "really paying off".
"We are getting a very good response," he said. "We have been advised by a number of firms that they are proceeding immediately with work they might otherwise have left until later in the year."
He said one firm has advised the N.E.S. office by letter this morning that work had been provided for 20 extra men. Another firm which plans to build a number of homes has decided to go ahead "as soon as possible", he said, without waiting for the frost to get out of the ground.
"These are typical of the response we have been getting to the publicity campaign the advisory committee sponsored," Mr. Turgeon said. "In addition many private home owners-

Unemployment
And these home owners are not Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation owners only.
-are hiring men for interior work. Some of the jobs may not be big but they are jobs nevertheless and all help to improve the unemployment situation."
Fort William congregations of all denominations Sunday heard an appeal from their clergy to join in the campaign and help provide employment "as an act of charity to your fellow man."
"No matter how large the job or how small," Mr. Turgeon said, "we have the men who can do it now rather than later when work will be more plentiful."
The McKellar general hospital, which built a large wing within the last three years, have decided not to wait until the summer to renovate the old part of the hospital. They joined in the "do-it-now" campaign, and they are doing it now. Plumbers, painters, paper-hangers and labourers are employed.
I know what unemployment is, Mr. Speaker, though not through personal experience, because I have never been out of work. However, I know that when a man is out of work he needs to eat, and sometimes he is job-blind. It is the duty of the government to do everything possible to provide work. I am sure the Minister of Labour is just as keen on doing this as is anybody who has spoken from the other side of the house. Everything possible must be done to get men work.
We have always had unemployment at the lakehead. When it freezes up, what happens? The deckhands and those who work on the boats are laid off. Elevator employees are reduced in number, as well as railway employees. Employment at the Great Lakes Paper Company Limited is cut down. It is our duty to do everything we can to get work for men.
I am asking this question of hon. members opposite, Mr. Speaker. Have you a "do-it-now" campaign in Regina? Have you a "doit-now" campaign in Winnipeg North Centre? Have you a "do-it-now" campaign in Hamilton? Have you a "do-it-now" campaign in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do you know how many unemployed there are in Fort William? There are 6,000.

I remember once seeing a picture of a boy helping a lame dog over a stile. Underneath were the words, "A little help with a lot of pity". I would just close by saying that a little bit of help, a little bit of action like that which has been taken by Fort William, is worth a great many telegrams and a great deal of talk.
' Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fort William told us that in his opinion the

government already have done a good deal for unemployment. That statement is probably quite true. But the fact remains that they obviously have not done enough. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre just mentioned, in the city of Fort William alone at this moment there are 6,000 people unemployed.
No.
The Canadian Press figures are here, and I saw them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the figure given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

It is a harsh and unpleasant fact that each year since 1951, this nation's army of unemployed has been increasing. In 1951 Canada had a peak of 296,000 unplaced applicants. In 1952 the figure increased to 382,000. By 1953 it was 408,000. Last year it was 570,000 and today it is over 600,000. In other words, Mr. Speaker, despite what has been said in this debate by the hon. member for Fort William and other Liberal members, the harsh fact is that unemployment is getting a little bit worse each year.
I feel that those figures are all the more disgraceful when we realize, first, that this trend is taking place at a time when Canada's national income is almost at an all-time high; second, that by almost any statistical standard we are living in one of the wealthiest countries in the world; and third, that the problem is less acute in other western countries which have fewer natural resources than Canada has. Most Canadians simply cannot understand why a country that can split the atom cannot put its people to work. They cannot understand, moreover, why this government, if it could solve the problem in wartime, finds it so complicated in peacetime.
I am not going to contend this afternoon that there is any easy or simple solution to the unemployment problem. I do not think there is any magic formula nor any pat answer. However, I am convinced that there are certain steps which the government could and should take and which, even if they would not solve the problems, would at least greatly alleviate it.
What are those steps? I found the speech made by the hon. member for Spadina earlier in this debate to be a good one, and one with which I could agree to a considerable extent. In the first place I agree with hon. members who have taken part in the debate and have urged substantial spending on public works. As I see it there can be no half measures in this connection. I am not going to dwell on the matter. I feel there is merit in such projects as a public housing program, a proper

highway system, slum clearance, conservation schemes and irrigation projects such as the South Saskatchewan river dam. In my opinion aggressiveness in this field could be a real stimulant to our economy at this time; it could be a shot in the arm.
But there is a second step which in my view would be even more effective in solving our unemployment problem. I shall contend today, as I have contended many times in the past, that the savage rates of taxation imposed by this government are having a good deal to do with the present slump in our labour market. During the debate one speaker after another has emphasized that if we are going to have full employment, consumers must have adequate purchasing power. Yet it seems to me that the present tax policies of the government are draining off purchasing power from consumers at an alarming rate. In 1954 the three levels of government in the country took 33 cents out of every dollar earned by the average Canadian. This government alone took 21 cents out of every dollar earned. The sums which the government is siphoning off in this manner would otherwise, I think, have been used by consumers to build homes, to buy automobiles, to buy farm machinery and to purchase clothing. I suggest that inevitably reduced purchasing power because of the level of taxation is reflected in reduced demands for labour.
The government is taking very large sums of money from people in the lower income groups in direct personal income tax. It is taking even more substantial amounts by indirect taxation. In Canada today, as every hon. member knows, we have a 10 per cent sales tax on almost every manufactured article except foodstuffs. We have a 15 per cent luxury tax on dozens of necessities. We have customs duties and tariffs. In my opinion these indirect taxes contribute very substantially to making Canadian prices among the highest in the world.
Take, for example, the automobile industry. As the house knows, the automobile industry is having unemployment troubles at the present time. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it any wonder? I have seen figures put out by the automobile industry which indicate that on a standard car manufactured in Canada there are today direct and indirect taxes approximating almost $600. That of course forces up the price of cars to a point where many labourers and farmers find it very difficult to buy automobiles. So it is with hundreds of other products. High taxes are contributing to high prices, high prices are contributing to decreased demands, and in
Unemployment
my opinion decreased demands are resulting in additional unemployment.
Therefore I suggest to the government, as a second step to alleviate unemployment, that it should reduce the tax burden on individuals, particularly those in the lower income groups. I propose first of all a cut in personal income taxes for all Canadians earning $5,000 a year or less. Second, I suggest a sharp cut in sales and special excise taxes. In my opinion such action would restore a good deal of purchasing power to Canadian consumers. In the third place-I speak personally now, and there may be few who will agree with me but I make the suggestion anyway-I suggest that the government should alter its tax policy in order to give greater encouragement to business expansion and investment. Today, as hon. members know, the standard rate of corporation tax is 49 per cent. In other words the government is taking roughly one-half of the profits earned by large companies.
If the Minister of Finance were here, even he would agree that such rates are pretty severe. He has said so publicly in the past. It seems to me fairly obvious that this high rate of taxation must tend to be harmful to the nation's investment program in new plant and equipment. Our population and our labour force are increasing rapidly each year. We have to depend on investment in new factories and new equipment to provide jobs for those added to the labour force. I should like to remind the Minister of Finance of a speech he made before the Canadian Tax Foundation on November 16 last, on which occasion he said:
In this country it is still left mainly to the private business world to plan expansion and development, to supply capital for new ventures, assume the financial risks and take the initiative in all the ways that provide employment and careers for those who work for salaries and wages.
In other words, the Minister of Finance said at that time that we still depend primarily on the business world to provide employment opportunities. If the Minister of Finance really believes that, and I am sure he does, I cannot understand why he continues to hobble industry in carrying out that responsibility effectively, by imposing on it such crippling taxation. To the extent that high taxes prevent either individuals or companies from expanding, new jobs are jeopardized. I am absolutely convinced that business would respond with increased activity and greater expansion if their taxation rates were reduced to more realistic levels. Speaking only for myself, I ask the Minister of Finance to contemplate such action as a

Unemployment
major step in combating unemployment. I believe the cut should be both deep and substantial.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to an experiment recently tried in the commonwealth of Puerto Rico. The standard of living in Puerto Rico is considerably lower than in Canada. One of the major problems they have had to deal with has been unemployment. In the past that country has had very heavy unemployment. In an effort to cope with it the government of Puerto Rico several years ago asked Mr. Beardsley Ruml, one of the foremost United States economists, and a few other advisers to come to Puerto Rico and look into the problem. They came up with a solution which I think is rather unique. I have in my hand an advertisement taken from Newsweek of February 28, and I should like to read a number of excerpts from it. It is headed: "Now Puerto Rico Offers 100 Per Cent Tax Exemption to New Industry". The advertisement goes on to say:
. . . "we do seek new and expanding industries". Federal taxes do not apply in Puerto Rico, and the commonwealth also offers full exemption from local taxes. That is why 300 new plants have been located in Puerto Rico, protected by all the guarantees of the United States constitution.
In a dramatic bid to raise the standard of living in Puerto Rico, the commonwealth government is now offering United States manufacturers such overwhelming incentives that more than 300 new factories have already been established in this sun-drenched island . . .
First and most compelling incentive is a completely tax-free period of ten years for most manufacturers who set up new plants in Puerto Rico.
The advertisement continues:
The commonwealth will leave no stone unturned to help you get started. It will build a factory for you. It will help you secure long-term financing. It will even screen job applicants for you-and then train them to operate your machines . . . Says Governor Munoz: Our drive is for new capital . . . The commonwealth is interested in attracting all suitable industries . . .
