I think that experiment has a great deal of merit, and I am going to send the advertisement to the Minister of Finance. Today in Puerto Rico almost 50,000 people who a few years ago were unemployed are working in plants which were brought to Puerto Rico because of the tax incentives offered by the government there. Perhaps the same kind of scheme would work in Canada, even if details had to be changed. I do think the government should examine that scheme thoroughly to see if the same thing could be of value here in Canada.
In combating unemployment we should consider giving tax exemptions to certain types of industry for a limited period while they are becoming established. If the minister thinks such a procedure is a little too extreme, I would certainly add my voice to

those who have urged that at least he allow accelerated depreciation on new plants. This method worked very successfully during world war II and during the Korean war, so I feel it should be equally successful at this time in encouraging employment.
I am convinced, too, that the fiscal weapon could be used to combat seasonal unemployment. One of the industries which is hardest hit at the present time is the construction industry. It is always so expensive to build in wintertime that most companies prefer to build in the spring, summer or fall. But there are many parts of Canada where construction can go on during the winter.
I am absolutely convinced that if the government would give contractors, or people who were building, tax incentives to construct in December, January, February or March, more building would be done. If tax incentives are not sufficient, then perhaps we should even consider subsidies. In the long run I feel it would be cheaper to take such action than to keep people on unemployment insurance during the winter months.
Today I have urged both greatly increased expenditures on the part of the government, and reduced taxation. I suppose some may argue that this is not being consistent. In speaking in parliament I have always urged strict economy in government spending, and I do not think I will ever change my views. I cannot concede that waste or duplication in governments is of any use to anybody. I cannot concede that it is fair to pay large subsidies to certain specific groups at the expense of others. Canadians are a thrifty people. I think most Canadians would like to see the budget balanced. But at this time I feel that more important than balancing the budget is the welfare of our Canadian citizens. Today our country is badly in need of a stimulant, even if in the process the government is forced into deficit financing.
In a period of full employment I feel the budget should show a surplus, and the bigger that surplus the better. Today inflation has been replaced by deflation. Business seems to be contracting, and full employment has been replaced by heavy unemployment. Thus I say that the considerations which formerly called for balancing the budget now point in the opposite direction. I say again that deficit financing, probably heavy deficit financing, could help to alleviate unemployment. This is no period for timidity. It is not a period for half measures. There are 600,000 Canadians out of work. Parliament must act quickly and with efficiency. Perhaps fiscal policy cannot end unemployment, but I certainly feel it can alleviate it.

The one man upon whose shoulders the responsibility must tall during the months ahead is the Minister ot Finance. I call on the Minister of Finance and the government to increase spending, decrease taxation and not fear a deficit budget.

A great number of members of the house have taken part in this debate on employment and unemployment, Mr. Speaker, and I feel it is one of the most important problems facing Canadians at this time. It is because of the importance of the subject that I rise to take part in this debate.
There are a good many angles to the unemployment and employment problem, and rather careful study is required to arrive at a solution that will be suitable to this varied economy. I am going to pause here a moment to point out to the government that Liberal members across the country, and some newspapers, are saying that already too much has been said about this unemployment question, and that in itself may cause some dismay and some hesitation on the part of individuals and industry. I want to point out also that in the 25 years since 1930 the Liberal party has never failed to try to saddle the Conservative government that followed the Mackenzie King government with responsibility for the depression and unemployment of that time. Even at this late date they still try to do that, so it apparently depends upon who is blaming whom whether or not it is a good policy.
There are three major factors, as I see it, that are causing unemployment, and for the most part they are the result of government policy or, shall I say, lack of policy. First of all the fiscal policy has priced us out of many markets, not only markets abroad but domestic markets. People in Canada are finding it difficult to purchase the things they need. I think our trade policy is probably the biggest factor in unemployment and the loss of markets. Our trade policy is inflexible; it is unrealistic, and it is largely controlled from beyond the shores of Canada, at Geneva. The third item is taxation at the federal level. It is so high that competitors are able to undersell us. When we add declining farm prices to this list, we find that the farmers are without the purchasing power they require. Many of the things the farmers have to buy are either high in price or increasing in price.
Just at this moment I have two or three quotations from newspapers that I wish to use to emphasize what I have already said. The first has to do with trade, and it is from the London Free Press of March 12, 1955.
Unemployment
The newspaper article is based on the report of the dominion bureau of statistics and it says in part:
Canada's share of an expanding world wheat market has declined.
Farther down it says:
Canada's exports dropped by 3,600,000 bushels to 135,100,000-
At another point it says:
During January, Canada's wheat exports totalled 17,900,000 bushels, down from 19,900,000 shipped in December-
There is an indication of a loss of markets, yet I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce was trying to indicate to the house that Canada's wheat trade was in a flourishing condition. Then in the Ottawa Journal of March, 1954, there was an editorial headed "Pricing Canada Out of Trade". This editorial quotes from the New York Times as follows:
The administration has two powerful anti-recession weapons at its disposal; easy money and tax-reduction incentives. Few will disagree, either in Wall Street or Main Street, that tax reduction probably would be the more effective at this juncture.
These words relate to the United States economy, but I was struck with their applicability to our own conditions. I just weigh those words because of my own look at the results of inflation and the certain amount of inflation that exists now.
You can increase employment by increasing the farmer's take-home pay, and the reverse is also true. I point out to the government that if they want to increase the army of unemployed, all they have to do is take measures to further reduce the income of the farmer by reducing or eliminating floor prices. If they do that they will have still more unemployed on their hands. There are approximately 600,000 unemployed, and there are at least 1,200,000 dependents of those unemployed, people who are no longer able to purchase in quantity the goods they otherwise would buy, and that is acting also as a brake on our economy. They are no longer able to purchase the products of either factories or farms. Right here I would point out that urban prosperity is closely linked with rural prosperity.
There are those in the country who believe that heavy taxation to level out income so those in the high income brackets can contribute to the well-being of those in the low income brackets can result in a levelling of poverty instead of a levelling of wealth. We can go too far along that road. In fact I think we have already gone too far, and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, who has just taken his seat, emphasized that very clearly.

Unemployment
I should like to quote from the London Free Press of March 8. The heading is: Farmers need intelligent aid measures
Canada's federation of agriculture representatives were certainly on sound ground when they drew attention of the federal cabinet to the cost price squeeze from which Canadian farmers are suffering. There is no doubt that farm prices have gone down during the last two or three years, while there has been no corresponding decline in costs.
Difficulties involving the farm population are serious, partly because of the number of farmers and their families, but also because farming is still so basic to our whole economy that agricultural depression tends to spread to many other parts of our system.
Since 1945 the government has failed to halt inflation. In fact, as I have pointed out more than once, the government has welcomed it because it brought more income to the tax collector and helped the former minister of finance with his buoyant revenues that he boasted about. Graham Towers intimated that a warning light might flash if our economy were in danger. I wonder very seriously whether his resignation was the warning flash he mentioned, because after his resignation the interest rate of the bank was reduced one-half of 1 per cent. Is this the needle of inflation? While there were protests to the contrary on the part of those in high places, it has not changed, as far as I and a good many other people in the country are concerned, the fact that it is an inflationary move.
I want to contrast that with the action of the Bank of England. Since the war the people in that country have been able to rebuild a nation and an economy that was practically down and out owing to the ravages of the war of 1939-45. Their policy has been almost the opposite of ours, and still is. It was indicated in the press not too long ago that the day was fast approaching when convertibility would be a reality.
The forecast of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that when the budget is brought down this year there is likely to be a deficit of some $50 million was an inflationary measure, even though it was only a forecast. I submit that we have already inflated our economy to the point where we have priced ourselves out of world markets. The Minister of Trade and Commerce forecast a very prosperous year in 1955. True, he said there would be some soft spots. I am wondering whether the 600,000 unemployed in this country like to be referred to as soft spots in the economy? Do the 600,000 unemployed and their 1,200,000 dependents think 1955 is likely to be a prosperous year? I doubt it very much.
The minister referred to Canada's vast natural resources. We had those vast natural

resources from 1926 to August 7, 1930, but they did not head off the depression and the unemployment of those days. From 1926 to August 7, 1930, were the days during which the government of Mackenzie King held office.
I wish to refer to another clipping from the London Free Press, and quote only part of it:
Cutting taxation is a positive and immediate stimulation to business, and government economy which permits real cuts in the amount collected from the taxpayers will be of great value.
They deal with the unemployment situation, which they say demands action. What is the government's policy on unemployment? A dominion-provincial conference on fiscal matters is mooted for April, but apparently there is to be nothing on the agenda about unemployment. Apparently the policy of the government is to say, let us sit this one out, or let us wait and see. So far not one really constructive suggestion has been brought forward. It is true that there was a commonwealth conference in Britain, but it has failed to inspire any confidence in the future so far as industry or labour is concerned. The Prime Minister's reports were platitudes, pious hopes and good wishes, but these things do not create jobs. I would say that they were void of any constructive policy on trade or fiscal matters.
I have two more clippings which indicate what is going on. The first is from the Financial Times of March 11, and the heading reads:
Ottawa buys armed forces tools abroad-industry irked.
They can be irked, but they dare not protest or they would not get a contract. Then "Tempus" had this to say in the same issue of the Financial Times:
The Liberals somehow have managed to keep the subject of falling export trade off the front pages and chances are that, with the new policy of inflation, they will have that job fixed by spring.
I would say that he is at least hopeful. No indication came from the commonwealth conference that the question of convertibility had been discussed or even thought about. The commonwealth conference ended just like the trip of the three travelling salesmen of the cabinet who journeyed to Washington early this year. The end results were nil. I again ask, what is the government's policy? The Minister of Labour will probably follow the lead of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and end up with Mackenzie King's infamous five-cent speech as a statement of policy. Probably they will hold a seance. It would be just as effective as conferences that have been held so far.

I return now to the municipalities, because after all they represent the grass roots of this country. The municipalities are staggering under a burden of taxation, and are rightly resisting and evading in every possible way responsibility for the care of the unemployed. They know that once they accept that responsibility the burden will never be lifted from their backs.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced a 1956 census. This will cost $5 million and will employ 15,000 people, but it will not add one iota to the wealth of this country. I never realized until I read about it that the agricultural industry of Canada was so important. The minister indicated that they are going to ask the farmers 75 questions as against 7 to be asked the residents of cities. Back in 1951 when they took the regular census 200 questions were asked the farmers and only 75 of residents of cities. I am going to suggest that the government add one more question to this list, and I suggest the following: What are the basic causes of unemployment? I venture to say that the 600,000 unemployed and the 700,000 farmers will come up with more correct answers than we have heard from the government.
When the resolution dealing with the grade crossing fund was being dealt with last night the hon. member for Waterloo North indicated twice in his speech that there was serious unemployment in his area. I think if all hon. members would tell the truth, like the hon. member, we would soon begin to realize how serious this situation is.
I want to return for a moment to the argument we hear so often that Canada has such vast natural resources that it does not matter what happens. I would point out that Switzerland is a country with few natural resources, but it has built up an economy by importing and exporting, similar to what Great Britain was able to do. This economy was built up through industry, labour and the employment of their people, not by unemployment.
We could take a lesson from history, and I need mention only two nations, ancient Rome and Spain. In their heyday those countries held the greatest natural resources known at that time, but they both went down the drain because they failed to employ their own people. They employed people outside their lands to make the things they needed, and where are they today?
There are indications that a great portion of Canadian resources are being shipped out of this country to be processed by labour in foreign lands, by foreign wage earners, while 50433-130
Unemployment
our people stand idle. Natural resources alone do not make a great nation; it is the industry of its people that makes a nation. Let it not be said that our natural resources are being used to keep people employed in other countries.
Before I close I should like to quote shortly from a brief submitted to the Minister of Finance by the Canadian institute of stove and furnace manufacturers. I quote as follows:
In warm air furnaces, Canadian production is down 6J per cent and imports are up 195 per cent.
And again:
Imports into Canada, in nine months only of this year, totalled 986 carloads of cooking and heating appliances.
If that is not an indication of a lack of foresight on the part of this government in protecting Canadian labour and ensuring jobs, I do not know what it is.
I should like to turn now to the annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada and the speech of Mr. James Muir. I am going to refer only to two or three quotations, where he is dealing with the unemployment problem. I wonder what Mr. Muir's reaction would have been if he had found in his pay envelope some six or eight months ago a little note saying "Your services are no longer required." I wonder what he would think if he found himself among the unemployed. I often wonder what people who are unemployed are thinking. It is quite easy when you are in a secure position like a member of parliament or like James Muir to pass this off lightly, but when you are out of work and hungry it is a different matter. Dealing with the economic welfare of Canada Mr. Muir had this to say:
The first of these is to ensure that our human resources are not wasted in involuntary idleness; that is, we should try to maintain a high and stable level of business activity and employment.
And again:
But general business stability has been continually threatened by inflationary pressure.
And further down:
The noticeable decline in exports since 1952 may also be attributed to a number of interrelated causes:	price declines, increased competition
from low cost producers abroad, the recovery of industrial capacity in war-torn countries, and the like. All these tend to alter relative cost and price relationships in the world market to Canada's disadvantage. But, in addition to the important matter of relative costs, a new factor has been injected by European suppliers who are able, with government support, to offer long-term financing to their customers in the world market. This type of financing is especially important in sales of heavy equipment; and, in one form or another, notably through the export-import bank of Washington, it has been available for many years to American export houses. We are aware that some very large foreign orders for equipment

Private Bill
which might have been obtained by Canadian firms, were lost to competitors during the year, largely owing to relatively favourable terms of payment.
I do not think we can say too much about this serious situation created by unemployment.

the second reading of Bill No. 244, to consolidate and amend acts relating to the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada.
He said: The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada was incorporated in 1908, and the act was amended in 1912 and 1929. That act is being repealed by the present bill, which is a consolidation bill. The royal institute will carry on under the same name and with its existing membership. There are only a few new clauses which do not affect directly or indirectly the privileges, rights or prerogatives of any existing body or any other profession.
The purpose of this bill is to facilitate the relations between the institute and various provincial associations of architects, and to add new powers in order to improve as much as possible the welfare of architecture in Canada and its various aspects. There are no other special details to be outlined, except to say that this bill indicates the importance of the institute and the classes of membership, and it enumerates the associations which will compose the institute. It establishes conditions under which the council of the institute can pass rules and regulations. There is also a modification in the value of real property which may be held, which has been increased from $200,000 to $500,000.
Architecture is the only profession, I think, which is not represented in this house. In view of the tremendous contribution of architects to the expansion of this country it is to be hoped that some day an architect will have the privilege of sitting in this house.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to endorse the principle of the legislation which is proposed. I listened with a great deal of care to the speaker who is proposing this legislation, and I noticed he indicated that no major change is proposed. I agree in part with his closing wish that some day we might have a registered architect as a member of this house.

I hope nothing I might say in the few minutes I intend to speak will be taken as a reflection on the institute or on any of the members of that institute or its affiliates. However, I have long felt that the legislators of Canada have a responsibility to the general public that supersedes any personal desire they may have for the advancement of a particular occupation or profession to which they may happen to be attached. I myself am a member of what is in effect a closed shop, the British Columbia teachers federation. I have heard on many occasions throughout Canada expression given to the feeling that the public welfare is not always adequately represented with those who wield a great deal of power wherever these institutions, associations or labour unions, if you like, exist.
I think the policy I wish to enunciate can be applied even to the closed shop labour unions. I hope the day is not too far distant when legislators in amending these acts will remember that the public welfare should also be represented in those who have charge of the administration of these professions or occupations.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. 126, to amend the Canada Elections Act (age of voters).

In speaking on this motion I wish to state at the outset that I give it my full support. This amendment would reduce the age of voters from the present 21 years of age to 18 years of age, with regard to federal elections.
The trend of the arguments which have been presented against this amendment have been to the effect that young people are not politically mature at the age of 18, and are unable to accept the responsibility imposed by the franchise. In fact someone quoted from a paper which stated that most 18-year-olds live in a world of hot dogs, popcorn, soft drinks and juke boxes, indicating that they were not sufficiently mature to accept this responsibility.
The same argument was used in the province of Saskatchewan when the provincial government introduced similar legislation to reduce the voting age in that province to 18. The opposition at that time referred to

this vote as the chocolate bar vote and contended that the government was endeavouring to take advantage of the youth. They spoke very strongly against granting this right.
I would like to point out that in wartime every young man of 18 is eligible for military training in Canada. In wartime we do not hear any talk about the immaturity of the young people. Young Canadian men who came from average Canadian homes astounded the world with their judgment and ability during the last two world wars. In fact it was the ability and the judgment of our young people which constituted a barrier which saved Canada and the world from the threat of fascism during the last two great wars.
I would also point out that if voting privileges are extended to people at the age of 18 it does not mean that every young person of 18 will vote at that age in Canadian elections. Elections are held only once every four years which means that only one-quarter of the voters would have an opportunity of exercising their franchise at the age of 18. Those who are 17 will not vote until four years later, when they are 21. This means that the average age of the young people voting for the first time will be 20 years of age.
I have watched Canadian youth in their colleges and universities. I maintain they are interested in the political life of Canada. They are interested in the history of Canada, and they understand democracy. In most provinces we grant young people of 18 the right to select their lifetime partner. That is a very grave step, but their judgment is not questioned. If they choose wrongly they have a lifetime in which to suffer as a result of their mistake. If they happen to make a mistake when voting they have an opportunity every four years to rectify the situation and make another choice.
I believe if young men and women are allowed to vote at 18 years of age they will have an interest in the proceedings in the House of Commons. They will be eager to see what their representatives are doing here, and whether or not they are speaking on behalf of the young people of the country. They will watch how the members serve and represent their constituencies. If they are denied the right of voting at 18 they can readily become indifferent to what is happening in parliament. As a matter of fact surveys have been made across Canada and their results reveal that a surprising number of Canadian people know very little about what happens in parliament, how parliament is conducted and what votes are taken here.
Canada Elections Act
I am definitely of the opinion that many of the speeches made in this parliament should be broadcast over a nation-wide hook-up in order to inform the people of Canada of what goes on here. I think such a move would help implant in the minds of the people a sense of their responsibility, and would give them actual knowledge by having them hear what goes on within parliament. By giving them the opportunity to hear some of the speeches, and the recording of the votes, they would be informed as to what the issues are.
At the present time the only sources to which they have access for information as to what is happening in the house are the copies of Hansard which are distributed daily, which they can procure for about $3 a year, and which take a great deal of reading; or the summarized reports which are carried in the daily press across the country, or the radio at news time. It would be much more realistic and would bring home to the people much more forcibly what happens here if, even for an hour or two each day in the months parliament is in session, there were broadcasts of the actual proceedings of this house, particularly when important issues are being discussed such as external affairs and unemployment, in order that the people might find out exactly what is going on in parliament.
That is something that is being done in the province of Saskatchewan at the present time. I would say that my own observation-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I dislike interrupting the hon. member, but I am afraid he is using a bill which has as its sole purpose a reduction of the voting age to discuss the merits of broadcasting or otherwise publishing the affairs of parliament. I am not suggesting there is anything objectionable in the hon. member's remarks, but if he is allowed to carry on along those lines I am afraid almost any subject under the sun could also be discussed on the motion for second reading of this bill.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was just going to point out that in my province we have found that it is the young people who are interested in what is going on in our own legislature. At the age of 18 people are more politically mature than the average person here believes them to be.
Oh, oh.

At any rate, all the arguments that have been presented against this bill have been to the effect that they are not politically mature. If hon. members opposite believe they should grant this voting privilege to people at the average of 20 years,

Canada Elections Act
they will have an opportunity of voting on the matter. When the vote comes I would suggest that they stand up and be counted. The arguments that have been presented have been largely to the effect that people at that age are politically immature. I suggest that this bill would be a good thing for Canada, a good thing for democracy and a good thing for this house.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: the hon. member for Assiniboia speaks now, he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the discussion when the bill was first moved, and particularly to the contribution made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pinard). I do not believe he dealt with the main argument I advanced in support of this measure, namely that young people 18, 19 and 20 years of age are sufficiently mature to cast an intelligent ballot and that, on any basis of comparison with those in any other age group in the country, they compare favourably indeed.
The bill makes provision for the age of 18.

Of course. I think the hon. member is capable of realizing that if anyone at the age of 18 is eligible to vote, anyone over the age of 18 is automatically also able to cast a vote.
I had hoped that arguments might have been directed to the question of whether or not young Canadians in that age group in fact have sufficient intelligence and sufficient knowledge to cast a responsible vote. I believe that they have sufficient intelligence and sufficient responsibility. I felt that the contribution made by the hon. member for Saskatoon was excellent. He advanced a number of arguments in favour of this bill that were not advanced by any other member who spoke. He pointed out that young people ordinarily reach maximum intelligence at the age of 15 or 16. He went on to explain that intelligence did not mean knowledge but something different, namely the ability to acquire knowledge. That being the case, I think it is reasonable indeed to ask that the voting age be reduced to 18.
Another excellent argument made by the hon. member for Saskatoon was that in relation to public affairs, as in relation to any other aspect of life, people learn by doing and that the way for young Canadians to acquire a better knowledge of public affairs is to have an earlier opportunity to develop such an interest. He went on to say that from his experience he thought it took from
fMr. Castleden.]
two to ten years after the age of 21 before most people became politically mature, and that since that length of time was necessary for people to reach political maturity he felt it would be a good thing for them to have the opportunity to vote at an earlier age, as they would therefore become politically mature at an earlier age.
I listened with great interest to the speech made by the Secretary of State. In his statement I do not think he advanced any important arguments-and I say this with great respect-against the proposition contained in this bill. As a matter of fact, as one looks over the remarks he made one will find that the Secretary of State does not advance any argument at all against the passage of this bill until he gets more than half way through his speech. For example, after he was well into his speech, as reported at page 1621 of Hansard, he said:
The sponsor of this bill has pointed out that my predecessor last year mentioned the question of expense. It is, of course, true that this consideration should not be a reason for opposing the measure.
Then he went on to point out that there would be some expense attached to the passage and the adoption of this measure, and that there would be expense attached to granting the vote to persons at the age of 18. The important sentence in that statement was this:
It is, of course, true that this consideration should not be a reason for opposing the measure.
If the matter of a small additional expense cannot be used as an argument for opposing the measure, I am wondering why that matter should be mentioned at all. If the matter of incurring additional expense is not a valid reason for opposing this measure, surely there was no point in the minister using this argument in his speech and, though not calling it a reason, apparently using it as an excuse for not supporting the measure.
He went on to say that he was of opinion that the provinces should take the lead in this question. Of course some of the provinces have already done so. He said he would like to see other provinces lower the voting age rather than see the federal government do so at this time. Then he said:
However, I do not want to put this forward as a reason for opposing the measure.
He wants the provinces to go first, but he says that is not a reason for opposing the measure. If we are to consider a vote on this subject in an intelligent manner, we should be given some reasons. If we are inclined to vote against it we should have some reasons and some arguments for doing so. We should not list a number of hypothetical

objections and then say these are not reasons for opposing the measure. The Secretary of State had this to say a little later:
We should deal with that matter first-
He was referring to making sure that more people over the age of 21 have in fact the right to vote.
-and so arrange things that as many Canadians as possible who come within the section of the act defining the voting age and the conditions of voting will be able to exercise the right of franchise.
I am all in favour of that. I am all in favour of making it possible for all those who have the right to vote under the act to cast their votes. The minister went on to refer to persons abroad at the time of voting as a group of Canadians eligible to vote who should, by amendment of the act, be given the right to vote. But surely the adoption of the bill would in no way affect or prevent action being taken along the lines suggested by the minister, namely all possible steps to see that the greatest number of persons possible who are eligible to vote do have the right and opportunity to vote on election day. I do not think the fact that certain necessary amendments must be made to the act can be advanced as a valid argument for turning down the bill now before us, which is merely a further amendment to the act.
The last argument of the minister with which I wish to deal was advanced in reference to a speech made by another member. He said he thought the age of majority should be studied before the age of voting is lowered. I do not think the fact that a person must be 21 years of age to sign many civil contracts can be advanced as a substantial reason for opposing this measure. As has been pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Yorkton, in a great many provinces young persons of the age of 18 are able to sign a very important contract, a marriage contract, that is considered valid under the law. If a person of the age of 18 can enter into such an important contract, then surely the argument is not valid that such persons should have to wait until the age of majority in order to vote.
We also know that under Canadian law persons 16 years of age and upward who are found guilty of murder may be hanged. If we are going to make persons responsible for such an act at such an early age and consider them adult in every respect when it comes to paying the death penalty, then we might consider reducing the voting age even though the voting age would then be lower than the age of majority. We also know that in most provinces a young person can obtain a driver's licence at the age of
Canada Elections Act
16 and operate a vehicle on our highways. With traffic accidents as frequent as they are in these days, that is certainly putting a great deal of responsibility on young shoulders.
As was suggested by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill) last year, I hope each member of the house, more particularly those on the government side, will cast his vote on the basis of his belief as to the merit of the measure, and will not be influenced in any way by a party decision. As the minister said last year, the election law should be a law of parliament as a whole and not a law based upon the decision of the government in power.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mrs. Fair-clough.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened for several days to hon. members from practically every section of the house expressing their views on this matter of unemployment. In my judgment this is one of the primary problems facing the country today. We hear a lot of talk in the house and over the air and we read a lot in the press about our way of life as against the way of life that is offered to us by another contending order. Our way of life is the way a person lives, how he is housed, how he can look after his family and what are his income and standard of living. There are 600,000 people in Canada today who are unemployed, and in their minds there may be growing shadows of doubt as to whether a change of some kind might not be beneficial.
In discussing this question of unemployment, when we say it is regional or seasonal or not serious, or use any of these other slogans, we are not helping the situation very much. I think hon. members of this house, particularly members of the government, have to take a square and objective look at the matter. Neither will a lot of acrimonious debate or name-calling do very much to help the situation. What I am going to try to do this evening is tell the house exactly what I think about it.
In 1939 there were 523,000 unemployed in this country and things were pretty serious, as that was 11-4 per cent of the then working force. Today there are more unemployed, and taking the country as a whole they represent about 6 per cent of the working force.

However there are many communities in the country where the unemployed number more than 11-4 per cent.
I think the time has come when instead of just trying to rationalize the problem and hoping for some miracle to happen we should provide some concrete plans to do something about it. In my judgment we have two alternatives. Either we go back to 1939, and we are pretty close to that, or we go back to 1945 and start to take some authority if the government is expected to have at least some say in the management of our economy. If we are not prepared to do that, then we are not going to do very much about unemployment.
In looking at the thing in a broad way, considering the country as a whole and who owns and controls the economy, one must realize that there is not much the government can do in connection with unemployment except to put patches on it here and there and provide cushions such as unemployment insurance, family allowances and so on. When it comes to telling General Motors or Dominion Steel and Coal or any of these other large organizations who actually control the economic processes of the country what they should or should not do, the government has no authority.
There are some hon. members in this house who are quite loud in their demands that the government do this and that. I am sure they realize as well as I do that the government has no power today to say anything to the people who actually control the economic processes of the country. When the government does attempt to take some authority they are the first to get on their feet and scream "dictatorship; the government should not have that authority." Only yesterday when the Minister of Defence Production asked for the continuation of certain powers that might be used in an emergency those same people, who today are ready to hurl accusations at the government and demand they do something, were the very ones who were on their feet screaming "dictatorship".
The Minister of Defence Production pointed out to the house quite clearly that in his judgment some controls of this kind were necessary if he and the government were to be expected to do something in the event of an emergency. As far as this group are concerned we realize that the government has to have some authority to direct and manage if it is going to do something about unemployment. While the democratic system exists and parliament meets we are not afraid to grant certain emergency powers to the government in order that they may do certain things. We always come back here and
Unemployment
examine the actions of the government in the light of what has taken place.
I said a moment ago that we either had to go back to 1945, when there were certain controls, or we had to go back to 1939. Press reports at this time indicate clearly that we are practically back to 1939. Many of us lived through that period, and we can remember press reports like this one which is datelined Whitby, Ontario, and states that three men were picked up after committing a robbery. It came out during the trial that they had gone out to try to get something for their children to eat, as there was not a bun or a loaf of bread in the house. Unemployment forced those men to become criminals, and for the rest of their lives they will bear the stigma of having been convicted. They are the victims of a faulty economic system. That is the kind of thing that was so prevalent in 1939, and there are all too many press reports like this today from various parts of the country.
Then I pick up another one which reminds me of 1939. This states that the mines will be on half time next week. I do not suppose these men will show in the total of unemployed, but since last November the coal mines of Nova Scotia have been working on a broken schedule of three days a week because of lack of markets and so forth. While the government cannot tell Dominion Steel and Coal when to work and when not to work they can at least avoid doing anything that aggravates the situation.
Yesterday I asked the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys why the subvention on the movement of coal from Cape Breton to Newfoundland was being discontinued. The answer I got was not an answer at all. I read it over again today and found that I did not get any reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: That is in force until the end of the month.

I hope it will be continued in force. This matter is not as unimportant as it may look. United States coal can be landed in Newfoundland at $2.40 per ton cheaper than DOSCO can put coal into Newfoundland. I do not know why but that is the actual fact. The subvention was put on to level off the cost and put Nova Scotia coal in a competitive position. That subvention was applied to the movement of 250,000 tons of coal into Newfoundland. If the subvention is withdrawn that coal will no longer be in a competitive position, and that market will be lost when it is very badly needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: We do not think it will be lost.

I hope the minister will continue that subvention. I hope he will see that

Unemployment
this market is not lost. I think I know some of the problems. I have been checking the matter since I spoke to the minister yesterday. Shipping facilities are not good. Boats that generally haul this coal are tied up in Sydney harbour while 10,000-tonners are being loaded. They stand there for a week at a time and charges pile up which are added to the total cost. On the other hand there are no storage facilities in Newfoundland. These are things which that company should provide. I mentioned that because I thought the subvention was being withdrawn, and I hope now it will not be.
Let us now approach this question from another angle. I hold the great majority of the people of Canada largely responsible for the situation which exists today. In the last election the people of this country had four choices; they could vote Liberal, Conservative, C.C.F. or Social Credit, in some parts of the country.
Or Clarie Gillis.

They fully understood what they were voting for. The government candidates clearly stated that they stood for the system of free enterprise. The Conservatives said they also believed in free enterprise, but added that they would make it freer. We made it quite clear straight across the country that as far as we were concerned, if we had enough members in this house we intended to change the mechanics of society to avoid a repetition of what occurred in 1939. The people of this country, however, voted for the government we have today by a huge majority, and gave that government a mandate to do exactly those things which they are doing now.
The unemployment situation last November was practically What it is today. When the by-elections were held in this country about 40 per cent of the people in the various ridings came out to vote and the other 60 per cent stayed home.
They were satisfied.

They were not interested, they were apathetic. Their attitude was, let Joe do it. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is how fascism began. If the Canadian people are not sufficiently interested in the affairs of their country to go out and exercise their franchise by voting for someone who will accomplish things for them; if they want to stay home and let someone else run the show and state they are satisfied with what little is being done, I am convinced that process will not continue for long. Someone will rise and say, "O.K., I will run it for you and from now on you Will do what you are told to do." I think a lesson must be taught the

people of Canada. It must be driven home to them that if they want democracy they will have to get out and work for it. If they want to avoid unemployment they will have to do something about it. If the government is doing nothing about it, then the people must elect a government which will do something about it.
While the hon. member for Prince Albert was speaking this afternoon and waving the green book containing the proposals of the government, I sat thinking to myself, "You are a little bit reckless in using that book." If there is any party which is vulnerable in so far as the 1945 dominion-provincial conference is concerned, the members of that party do not sit far from me.
I remember the dominion-provincial conference of 1945, because I was interested in it. At that time the dominion government proposed to take the responsibility of looking after the employable unemployed, and also offered the people of Canada a health program to be paid for by the federal government which would have been put in operation from coast to coast. This would have been one of the biggest assets in this country today had that proposal been accepted. However, neither proposal was accepted because three provinces wrecked that conference. It will be a long time now before these proposals can be put into effect.
The hon. member for Prince Albert should have remembered that conference when he was speaking this afternoon, and he should have remembered the people who wrecked that conference. The proposals at that conference were the last evidence he should ever have used in this house to justify his criticism of the government in the matter of unemployment.
I have heard it stated by hon. members on my right that there is no unemployment in New Zealand, Australia or in Britain. The hon. members who mention this make no attempt to tell us why this is so. New Zealand elected a Labour government in 1935 and abolished unemployment at a time when we were confronted with it. Australia has had a Labour government for many years, and Great Britain formed a Labour government following the war which had to deal with the aftermath of war. The Labour governments in Great Britain and the other countries changed the mechanics of society in those countries and set machinery in motion which has not been touched since by succeeding governments. They succeeded in abolishing unemployment, and the machinery which was set up is still there.
The same thing could be done in this country providing the government were given

a mandate to do it. When you run on the ticket of free enterprise, however, and receive a mandate from the people of the country on that ticket, then you have to follow the rules of the game as they are until such time as the people of the country give you a mandate to change them. The reason there is no unemployment in Britain, Australia and New Zealand is that the mechanics of society were reset to meet the needs of a modern world. In Canada we continue to jockey along in the old style of 1867, instead of changing the constitution to suit the times.
The chamber of commerce frequently advances a reason for unemployment in these words: "The answer is very simple; labour is pricing itself out of the market. That is the answer. Wages are too high." That is not a sound argument at all. It is merely an excuse which cannot be justified. If you examine the import-export picture of the last few years you will find it is not the low-wage countries where we have trouble in marketing our goods, it is the country which has the highest wage structure in the world, the United States, where we conduct about 60 per cent of our export-import trade. Last year, in 1954, we had an unfavourable trade balance with the United States of some $758 million. Wages in Canada are much lower than in the United States. On the other hand we had a favourable trade balance with Britain and other non-dollar countries of some $633 million, which enabled us to emerge at the end of 1954 with a very small deficit in our trade balance. The argument that labour is pricing itself out of the market does not hold water.
Let us look at the other side of the picture. I think profits might have something to do with it, and I think the proper industry to examine is the farm implement industry. One of the biggest factors in the unemployment picture today is a 44 per cent drop in farm income. I have examined figures relating to the farm implement industry for the period 1945 to 1951, which were the latest figures I could get. In that industry in 1945 the wage share of the dollar was 42-4 per cent. In 1951 the wage share of the dollar in that industry had dropped to 29-9 per cent. Wages came away down in the farm implement industry, and the profit picture in 1945 for the entire industry was about $1,500,000. By 1951 the profit picture in that industry had changed and had risen to $13 million, or an increase in profits of approximately 700 per cent, while the wage share of the dollar had declined from 42-4 per cent to 29 per cent. If anyone is pricing himself out of the market it is the group of money grabbers who want to
Unemployment
skyrocket those profits and share them among themselves, regardless of the best interests of the country.
We hear much talk to the effect that we want export markets. What about the home market? You never hear anyone say anything about the unmet needs of the people of Canada, and there are plenty of them. If we met the needs of the people of this country we would not have any unemployment. The few items I have listed here were taken from the last census. There is a tremendous market for these things if we could meet the needs of this country. For example, in the matter of housing, we need at least half a million dwellings in order to catch up on our accumulated backlog. Of the dwellings we have, the 1951 census showed that 940,000 were either overcrowded or in need of major repairs or both; that 900,000 had no inside running water; that almost 1,500,000 had no bath or shower for exclusive family use; that over 1,200,000 had no flush toilet; that nearly 600,000 had no hot water supply.
In a modern age in a country like Canada that is a rather terrible picture. I do not say the government can undertake a proposition of that kind, but what is the matter with the appliance industries? What is wrong with those who make and supply that type of equipment? Surely they have brains enough to organize the means whereby these facilities could be supplied and financed through some kind of company, so people could be put to work supplying these modern facilities. But nothing is done about it. Oh, no; we want free enterprise. We want to come to the government. We want a guarantee on every line. We want a guarantee of this, that and the other thing. There is no longer risk capital. Enterprise is no longer free, and it is no longer enterprise. It is a straight gangster machine with an economic gun at the head of the government, still trying to extract profits and at the same time get guarantees for whatever it may put into it.
The same thing applies in the appliance industries in connection with stoves, refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners, furnaces, telephones and so forth. These things are no longer luxuries; they are necessities in this modern age. If an industry is turning out commodities of that kind, with a market readily available at home, then I think they should have a proper sales organization and proper financing methods so as to make this equipment available to the people of Canada over a long-term period. But no; they want someone else to go out and do the selling for them.
The easy thing to do today is borrow money from the government, with an accelerated depreciation clause in the contract

Unemployment
so these costs will be written off in four or five years without their paying anything. They say, we will get it in that way; we will improve our plant and equipment; we will put in more modern devices. We will get more production with fewer men. We will make men the slaves of machines instead of machines the slaves of men. All that modern technological advances are doing today is creating misery on the one hand and huge profits on the other, throwing men onto the streets. It is not much of an argument for modernization, but that is exactly what is happening.
The steel plant in Sydney borrowed money from the government, as did Algoma and the others. They modernized their plants. There is no expansion; they maintain the same ratio of production, but they put 1,600 men on the road. That kind of thing is not good enough. I think it is time for the people of this country-and I hold the people responsible-to wake up and demand the kind of machinery in the hands of government whereby there could be brought into society some regulation that would protect people, instead of figures on the right side of the balance sheet in the ledger for someone who did not think enough of the country to provide those who produce the wealth with at least enough food, clothing and housing.
As I think about those people, Mr. Speaker, I often wonder what kind of minds they have. Do they ever stop to realize that they are passing through this world only on a short visit, and that when they take out the time occupied in sleeping the visit is extremely short; that while they make millions, some day they will have to lie down on a bed by themselves, without any executive board, and must close their eyes and say, "Now I meet the unknown future"? That is the end. There are no pockets in their shrouds. There is no balance sheet over there, because they burn up, where most of these people go. I think it is nearly time that lesson was driven home to those people.
I think there are many things the government can do. At a time like this I do not think the tax relief which was advocated this afternoon is what is required, because I would judge that those who advocated tax relief meant tax relief for corporations. What for? So they will expand their businesses? Then this other fellow says, "What do they want to expand them for? Their inventories are piled sky-high today. They do not know what they are going to do with them." If you give tax relief in order to pile up more goods, no solution is to be found there. The kind of tax relief that is needed is the
[Mr. Gillis.l
stepping up of exemptions in the lower income tax brackets. That is the place where the relief is needed.
The problem today is purchasing power. You must get that purchasing power in the hands of the people. In my judgment there is no other way in which the problem can be solved under our present scheme of things. The first step is to increase these exemptions. The second thing is to increase family allowances and old age security pensions. The government should accept 75 per cent of the responsibility for the trans-Canada highway, at least in the provinces that are in the have-not category. Quebec and Ontario may be able to meet the cost on a 50-50 basis-
We do that now.
No, you do not; not at all. The province buys the right of way.

I think the federal government should, to a greater extent, assist in that financing. As to the St. Lawrence seaway, now that it has gone through in spite of my opposition I think the government should speed up its construction and get it under way.
The matter of getting something done is, to my mind, a simple one. Maybe I am simple-minded. I think all the government needs to do is this. The statistics are available. First they should take a look at the inventories in the country or the surpluses that are on hand, the production that is lying there that cannot be purchased. I refer to surpluses in foodstuffs, in appliances, housing and so forth. Once they find out just what surpluses they have on hand, the next thing they should do is ascertain the amount of purchasing power that must be put into the hands of the people in order to buy back those surpluses, get them off the market and get the young productive workers back to work producing more goods.
This is the way to do it, and it is not my scheme at all. The United Nations has the best economists in the world, and they tell us that when over 5 per cent of your working force is unemployed you are getting into trouble and something should be done about it. The something that should be done about it is exactly what I said a moment ago. They advise the priming of the pump, the increasing of social security benefits so as to get purchasing power in the hands of the people and keep things rolling until such time as conditions change and more favourable winds blow.
But there is no permanent solution to be found for any of these things in public works. Such works are good. They create new

wealth, but they are only palliatives and the condition will arise again once they are finished. Today the labour content in any public works program is so small that it does not help very much. For example, when the Canso causeway was being advocated in 1942 I was a member of the reconstruction committee, and I heard the estimate made that it would take 1,500 men three years to build the causeway. With the equipment that was used it was built in 18 months by 262 men. The same thing will be found equally true of the St. Lawrence seaway project.
Now they are unemployed.

Yes, they are unemployed. There is no permanent solution in public works. We have to get down to brass tacks and do the kind of thing that was done in Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain. We have to assume some control of our finances. The old Bank of England was nationalized, and even Churchill did not denationalize it. The present government of England is making use of the changes the Labour party brought about.
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) eulogized Sweden today. He did not stop to think that Sweden has had a socialist government for a good many years. Certainly Sweden has no unemployment, and she will not have any. Unemployment
Back to Quebec!

In the past three years employment in this country has decreased alarmingly and all Canadians, with the exception of the government, have noted that fact. The official opposition, ever since the opening of the twenty-second parliament, has consistently warned the government against growing unemployment. As far as I am personally concerned, I have not missed a single opportunity of telling the house that, in my own constituency of Quebec West and throughout the Quebec district, more and more people were out of work and that the situation was becoming most alarming.
But the government steadily refused to see or to grasp the seriousness of the situation and constantly refused to discuss it. I have myself been accused more than once of quoting exaggerated figures. And yet I have certainly realized afterwards, and realize even more at this moment, that I had been right then, and that my statements had been correct.
This reminds me of a question I directed, about this time last year, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). I asked if the government intended to do something to help the
22,000	unemployed we had at the time in the Quebec area.

(Text):
What a man! (Translation):

I was nonetheless convinced that I was right and that there was nothing exaggerated in my statements. Official statistics confirmed them when, less than two weeks later, they showed that more than 21,000

persons were jobless in the Quebec and Levis district alone.
Under pressure exerted from all parts, the government, after standing aloof for too long a time in the face of the sad situation in which labour finds itself, finally agreed to discuss this thorny question, which should have roused the authorities out of their complacency.
Yet, members on the other side of the house continue to consider this problem as unimportant and seem by no means inclined to adopt the necessary measures to bring an early end to the sad predicament of more than half a million workers.
The Minister of Labour keeps on making statistical speeches and persists in saying that conditions are not as described by this side of the house. He refuses to use any other basis than the incomplete statistics collected by his department and relies solely on them to refute the arguments of the opposition and all those who take a real interest in the sorry plight of our workers.
As to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), he clings desperately to his out and out optimism, and imparts it to the cabinet, whose master and guide he is, in order to better hide from the nation the gigantic failure of this baleful administration wherein he personally controls, in dictatorial fashion, the whole Canadian nation's economy.

No, no.

This government is not concerned with the distress of our working people, or with the anguish of an important section of our people, or with the pain and want which are felt in our Canadian homes. The only thing it is concerned with is its own deep satisfaction of being able to stay in power to the advantage of a political party but to the disadvantage of the community.
Come now, this is nonsense!

From the very start of this debate, Mr. Speaker, we have heard moving descriptions of the state of affairs in various parts of the country, and we come to the con-

elusion that things cannot remain as they are any longer and that this government must act quickly to prevent the general disaster which seems inevitable.
If the situation is grave everywhere, there is no region more severely stricken than that of Quebec, and more particularly the riding of Quebec West which I represent in this house. A look at the past shows that history is repeating itself. Quebec has always been the first to suffer from the unemployment crises which we have had to face, with their aftermath of desolation, suffering, hardship, sorrow and malnutrition. Unemployment has created and still creates every condition calculated to cause the nation's misfortune, to strip people of hope and to inspire fear of the future. Suffering and hardship will not strengthen a population since the morale of a human being can withstand suffering only for a definite period of time, especially when he realizes that he is surrounded by riches. Those riches, put on earth by Providence, must be used to further the happiness and the prosperity of all, and the average worker is understandably unable to see how the people responsible for the development of those resources choose to use them for the benefit of a few, when the mass of the population is starving. Is that why Premier Duplessis is giving away all the forest resources of his province?
If my hon. friend is so able, why did he not try to win a seat in the Quebec legislature?
He has no time to waste.

No, because everything is done.

Figures never had the virtue of changing an actual condition, particularly when an attempt is made to use them for masking the truth. And the truth is, Mr. Speaker, that in the city of Quebec, at this time, in the city of Quebec alone, there are more than

20,000	unemployed, 13,000 of whom live in my county of Quebec West, while the others are mostly in the Prime Minister's county.
Now I know that the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) will try to refute me by quoting the figures supplied to him by the unemployment insurance commission, and I also know these statistics as well as he does. But I repeat that those figures in no way reflect the true conditions.
A certain number of workers are not eligible for unemployment insurance, and thousands of others cannot get the benefits because they have not accumulated enough working days.
As unemployment in the Quebec district has kept growing at an almost fantastic pace, and has spread to every season of the year, the government is ill-advised in contending that it is seasonal. This unemployment situation, Mr. Speaker, has now become permanent, alarming, ruinous. Not only does it jeopardize in our district the welfare of our workers and their families, but it threatens, to a great extent, the economic activity in our whole district.
The number of salaried people in the Quebec-Levis metropolitan area is estimated at 121,000 approximately, of which 100,000 at least are to be found in Quebec city alone. Since the end of the war, the percentage of people applying for jobs, in our metropolitan area, has been one of the highest of any area. This condition has been reflected, since the end of the war, in the tables published by the federal Department of Labour in the "Canadian Labour Market", and also in the monthly tabulations of the Labour Gazette under the title of "Labour Market by Districts".
It is obvious that unemployment, in the metropolitan district of Quebec, is not merely seasonal, it is a chronic, frictional unemployment, which is due, I believe, to permanent factors such as:
1.	The geographical situation of our district, the last great urban centre in eastern Quebec, which receives a regular flow of rural workers who come from the east;
2.	The coming on the labour market of a great many young people, more numerous each year.
There are many other factors to which I shall refer later on.
That additional manpower adds greatly to our labour force from year to year, far more than what the local economy can do to absorb it.

Unemployment
Of course, the Canadian government has set forth a policy of full employment throughout the country, and proposed to carry it out. But the truth is that it has made a pitiful failure of it.
Nobody in Canada can forget these words of the Prime Minister-which were so pointedly recalled the other day by my distinguished colleague from Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) and by my no less distinguished colleague from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker)-and I believe they should be quoted again because the man who uttered those words may try to forget them. I quote the Prime Minister:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent.
Mr. Speaker, never have I been more fully in agreement with the Prime Minister in awarding him this certificate of pathetic incompetence in the management of government affairs.
What a judge!

In view of his complete, total failure, there is nothing left for him to do, after making this general confession, but to abandon public life and the managing of the government and to let others, abler and better intentioned, settle this serious problem without delay.
The present federal government seeks to shirk its responsibilities and lay on the shoulders of the provinces the burden of remedying this situation. We have never seen so much smugness on the part of a government, unaware of its responsibilities and lacking courage to face them. That is a very sad realization for men who think themselves infallible and who do not dare tackle problems that might prove embarrassing for the political future of their party.
We should at least have enough heart and conscience to stop playing politics when the misery of our fellow citizens has reached its limit. The federal government will soon realize that it cannot indefinitely play on the feelings of our fellow citizens, because there comes a time when they react. The government would not dare at this time go before the people on this matter, because it would suffer a defeat such as it had never thought possible.
Let government resort to any argument, the fact remains that unemployment comes under federal jurisdiction. In that connection, may I quote some quite sensible remarks from Notre Temps of March 5, 1955:
[Mr. Dufresne.l
Unemployment is a Federal Responsibility
From a constitutional point of view it is clear that the question of unemployment is a federal responsibility. The federal government admitted as much during the 1930-1936 depression. It recognized its duties in that regard through the institution of unemployment insurance which ensures the jobless a meagre pittance when they fall upon evil days. Let us not becloud the issue. Let the federal government concern itself with its own responsibilities and let us also see to it that the provinces retain what is theirs by virtue of the constitution.
For my part I find that these attempts at confusing the issue are strange indeed. The federal government, whose centralizing practices are growing apace, is very prone to make grants to universities, to grant scholarships and to worm its way even into the educational field. But it is slow in recognizing its own proper responsibilities. It should leave education to the provinces and look after the jobless. This would be more normal, and safer too.
I am far from being opposed to a general national conference where representatives of the federal government, the provinces, the employers and the workers would meet to set up a coordinated plan for an efficient attack upon unemployment.
But if the federal government wishes to enlist provincial co-operation, it should at least ensure that the provinces enjoy those sources of revenue which they need to carry out their new social obligations.
Once again, unemployment is showing up the weaknesses of centralization. In a country as large as this, the Ottawa government can hardly take steps to relieve unemployment in a particular locality. The first responsibility, in this connection, belongs to the municipality, then to the provincial government and finally to the federal government. The latter has not wished it to be so. It has centralized sources of revenue and fiscal powers. It is now up to it to demonstrate in a practical way the alleged advantages of this policy of centralization it has foisted upon the provinces. The virtues or failings of any political system can only be judged by its performance.
The government has certainly failed in tact and ability when, on the very last day of the provincial session in Quebec and with the evident intention of confusing the issue- and public opinion by the same token-the provincial Liberals, in Quebec, initiated a debate on this matter in the legislative assembly.
Order!

This clumsy attempt was no doubt inspired by their Ottawa masters, from whom they get their orders.
The Liberal party, Mr. Speaker, is ready to resort to all kinds of schemes and to the worst contradictions for the sake of its own safety, even at the expense of the interest of the Canadian nation. Its contradictory attitude on this matter is glaring and hardly creditable, and, as it will be seen later, deserves the disapproval and contempt of all those who care for frankness and truth.
If honesty towards the electors is the proper basis for statements of policy, let us

realize, once and for all, that the electorate, purposely ill-informed by some unscrupulous politicians, should not be used as a stepping-stone for the rise to power of a political party, no more than the electors should be considered as puppets or jumping jacks in the pay of some politicians.
The elector is a citizen who deserves respect from his representatives and we, representing him in this house, have no right to make fun of him or to mislead him deliberately. I urge the government to ponder over this before calling upon themselves the vengeful anathema of this electorate who can no longer be laughed at with impunity.
I wish to thank the Toronto Globe and Mail for giving me an opportunity of bringing to light and to the attention of the country a contradiction on the part of the Liberals which I shall not qualify, as the only terms that I could use for that purpose would be unparliamentary. However, I reserve the privilege of qualifying it in my own words when the opportunity arises outside this house.
As you usually do.
The Toronto Star-
Knave! Sneak!

The Toronto Star, on February 26 last-there are some who have plenty of courage, Mr. Speaker, but not enough to speak on behalf of their constituents, of those whom they represent, those who, in their constituencies, are hungry, cold and often undernourished. They do have the courage to interrupt men who do their duty as representatives.

Ottawa, it said, is responsible for unemployment. Ottawa should pay the cost of relief. Ottawa can do something to relieve the hardships of the jobless.

Ottawa, "like an eternal spider" is creeping into the lives of all our people through its customs tariffs and its taxes which burden every business. The whole thing must rest1 on the shoulders of Ottawa and the federal government.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the way the Liberal party, through its press, deals with responsibilities and bestows them on whom it chooses, provided it can free itself from them and have someone else shoulder them.
Why does it act that way, and why would it have our Canadian people believe that unemployment has become a provincial responsibility? The answer is very simple. It is that in 1935 Ontario had a Liberal administration, Mr. Hepburn's, while Ottawa had a Conservative administration, Mr. Bennett's. Now that the situation is reversed, and that Ontario has a Conservative administration headed by Mr. Frost while Ottawa has a Liberal administration, this government wants the provinces, which it deprived of all their income sources, to shoulder the responsibilities it lacks the courage to face.
Mr. Lapalme, head of the Liberal party in the Quebec legislature, is doing the same as the Toronto Star and the Liberal party in Ottawa. This stand is just the opposite of the one advocated by Mr. Alexandre Taschereau, in Quebec, in 1935.

We will let the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker, pass judgment on such inconsistent stands which show a complete lack of frankness, as well as on those who are responsible for such inconsistency.
To come back to the alarming unemployment situation in the city of Quebec, and more particularly in Quebec West and Quebec East, let me state that that situation is one of the worst tragedies suffered by our people since the dark days of 1929.
There are some who will say, I know, that the setting up of unemployment benefits has been of considerable help to those who were periodically unemployed. I am not questioning that, even though benefits have never been anything but a means of providing partial support to those who have been forced out of work. It is certainly not a means to cope with unemployment or to get around a critical situation, as benefits paid to the unemployed only prevent them from dying of starvation and are paid only during a limited period.

Unemployment
Before resorting to the measures necessary to give back to our economy its full wartime vitality, and to the unemployed a steady and permanent job, we ought nevertheless to provide a temporary solution to the problem. The only remedy would be a program of public works of the same magnitude as the problem that we have to face today.
The public works program intended for Quebec city, to which the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) referred recently, is in no way likely to meet the situation. It consists in the construction of some buildings for which two-thirds of the amount appropriated will be used in buying materials. The balance will go to labour, which therefore will be very limited. Only a few will find employment and only for a short period of time.
Let us hasten to give the necessary orders so that the large projects which I have been requesting in the house since I came here for the first time, almost two years ago, might be undertaken without any more delay. I am not the only one who has been asking for these public works. They were requested on several occasions by the Quebec city municipal council and all important public bodies.
Last year, His Worship the mayor of Quebec city, when the unemployment situation was already alarming in our district, rushed to Ottawa, and urged the federal authorities to bring some relief to our fellow citizens. And according to the reports then published in the press, the answer he got was that, in a year or two, there was a possibility that Ottawa might contribute to a certain extent to the implementation of certain projects. There is a proverb, Mr. Speaker, which says that time heals everything. However, may I point out to the Prime Minister and to the government that this proverb does not apply to this particular case. According to its haphazard policy of wait and see, the government, no doubt, thought that time might bring an improvement in the employment situation which might silence those who suffer and appease their minds. Once more, the government has walked into the trap for, instead of improving, conditions are getting much worse from day to day. We have now reached the point when our welfare organizations, like the St. Vincent society, our public welfare services, our family welfare association, and all our charitable institutions cannot meet the situation. With poverty and hardship increasing as they do, the government will

soon be held responsible for the one and only increase, that of funerals in the city of Quebec, funerals of the victims of hunger, cold and malnutrition.
I note that some members on the other side of the house seem amused.
If you could only see the smile on the face of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer).
Yet, I would like to see them change places for some time with those poor workers at home, who are not paid the $10,000 we voted ourselves here.
And which you wanted yourself.
And which I did not want, as I opposed the bill. I know my responsibilities.
