Again I repeat that the only projects-urgent projects-that are needed, if we want to preserve the health and life of our fellow citizens, are the purification of the waters of the Lairet river, the deepening of the St. Charles river bed and the elimination of level crossings. You could add to this the rebuilding of our docks in the port of Quebec, that are disintegrating rapidly and will soon fall to pieces.
I shall probably be told that there are no funds available for these projects. There is nothing new in this, for as we find huge sums of money to make war, I do not see why much less considerable amounts could not be raised for the protection of all that is most dear to us, that is, our human resources.
Will the hon. member allow one question?
Certainly.
Is the hon. member aware that he belongs to the Progressive Conservative party, and that according to his party, there was never enough money spent for war purposes?

Mr. Speaker, I am not here to bear all the sins of Israel, but to speak for myself. I know very well that if my party

had been in power during the last war and had done only half the things the Liberal government did, the most powerful machine guns would have been brought out to shoot us.
If the government does not wish to vote the amounts required for the completion of the works I just mentioned, why does it not seek permission to use a portion of the hundreds of millions collected through the unemployment insurance contributions, millions which after all came from the employers and the employees of the country. Our people would thus obtain work, since I am convinced they do not wish to live on public charity. Being in a position to earn an honest living, they would contribute to the expansion and to the prosperity of the economic life of our district.
This year, we are contributing $26 million to the Colombo plan and we are glad to do so. Not a single dissident voice was raised in this house when that item was voted, since its aim is to enable poorer countries to raise their standard of living and to carry out various works for the protection of public health. That is a most praiseworthy endeavour, I admit. What I cannot understand, however-and I am speaking here for everybody in Quebec I have met-is that Canada, using the taxpayers' money, has irrigation work done in India, has infectious swamps drained because they constitute a danger for the health of Indian people when, right in the midst of Quebec city, in the heart of the riding represented here by the Prime Minister, two foul rivers are flowing, two real open air sewers, whose stench is no less foul and which are a source of most dangerous germs which the wind carries to the population. I do not object to the work we do to protect the health of human beings living thousands of miles away and I am not asking for a rigorous application of the saying "Charity begins at home" but I believe that it would be more logical to protect at the same time the health and the life of those whose daily work contributes to the greatness and prosperity of Canada.
Public enemy No. 1 in Canada today is therefore unemployment, which is becoming a real epidemic. Such a tragedy cannot last any longer and I will say to the government that it is urgent that a solution should be found to this distressing problem and since there can be no further delay the appropriate steps must be taken now, not in April when the preliminary federal-provincial conference, which will be simply a prelude to a similar conference to be held in the fall, will take place.

We cannot have a large portion of our population remain in the most absolute destitution for months to come. Since unemployment is above all a federal responsibility, I ask the federal government, in conclusion, to get busy as soon as possible with the solution of its problem.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would like to direct a question to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat.
You have my permission.

Does the hon. member
know that, under the constitution, the provinces could undertake public works coming within their jurisdiction to help alleviate unemployment which may exist in certain areas?
That is what they are doing all year round.

Mr. Speaker, the provinces surely can, under the constitution, if they wish to do so and if they have the means to do so, undertake works to take care of the alarming unemployment situation, but they are unable to do it now because the government which administers the affairs of the nation has taken over the sources of revenues of the provinces.

In other words they have attempted to use the problem of unemployment as a political football. They have advanced no practical solution and, may I add, it is certainly not in the speech made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) any more than in that of the hon. member for Quebec West that we can look for interesting or practical ideas.
It is inaccurate and absolutely contrary to the true facts of the case to claim that the government have not concerned themselves with the problem of unemployment. It would be just as inaccurate to claim that the government have refused so far, or still refuse, to carry out their responsibilities in the present circumstances.
The people of this country have put their trust in us and that trust is justified by the frankness and willingness with which we face up to this problem. There are serious difficulties in the field of employment, but the reason we are here today is precisely to eliminate these difficulties.
On March 1, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) described the situation in a masterly way. He is confident and again the future will prove him right. Unemployment should be considered in relation to the other perspectives of our economy. In fact, the level of employment must not be taken as the only yardstick of the prosperity of our country. If we consider the prosperous and sound situation in other sectors, we are justified to suggest that the unemployment situation will correct itself shortly. In fact it has already begun to do so. I am informed that, for the first time since last January, there has been clear evidence of an increase in the demand on the part of employers in the various offices of the employment service of the unemployment insurance commission in Montreal.
Contrary to statements made by pessimists of the opposition, the number of jobs continues to increase in Canada. However, the increase in population has been more rapid than that of available jobs. If proof of our industrial and commercial expansion is required, we only have to realize that, since the end of the war, more than a million immigrants-of whom more than half were workers-have been added to our people, hundreds of thousands of veterans have come back to their jobs in civilian life, and hundreds of thousands of young men and young girls have become old enough to work and are now part of our labour force.
In the face of such figures, the employment situation is amazingly good, and we are justified in being confident in the immediate future of this country.
I know that public works are but a palliative to the present situation. However, they constitute one of the means we have to fight unemployment. I therefore ask the government to start those works as soon as possible; the matter is urgent. I hope that the St. Lawrence seaway project will soon be in full swing which should improve substantially the situation in Montreal and in the south shore district.
Once more, as I did a month ago in this house, I ask that another bridge be built in Montreal at the foot of Pie IX boulevard. I do not ask for such a bridge in order to improve the traffic situation in Montreal-which is a purely municipal matter-but in order to avoid the chaos which the establishment of the St. Lawrence seaway will bring about. If steps are not taken right now to provide for the extraordinary development of the south shore, which in a few years will be changed from an agricultural section into an industrial and residential area, and if this
[Mr. Desehatelets.)

third bridge is not built as soon as possible, Montreal might find itself in a few years from now in an inextricable situation.
My suggestion, which is designed to help the eastern section of Montreal, would nevertheless be in the national interest; I feel indeed that such an important improvement would eventually benefit the whole country.
I understand the government has contributed towards the construction of a sports centre in St. John's, Newfoundland. They could also help the authorities of the city of Montreal to complete the construction of the sports centre on Pie IX boulevard in the constituency of Maisonneuve-Rosemont. This sports centre will be something unique in America.
Those are important public works which would help fight unemployment in Montreal.

To help the unemployed, particularly during the winter months, the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended earlier this session to provide for an increase in the duration and scale of supplementary benefits. A major revision of this act is proposed during the present session.
The position of the unemployed who have exhausted their benefits and cannot find work is certainly a matter for concern, particularly when they are the heads of families, and any amendment to this legislation that would bring these people some relief would be welcome and would greatly help our municipalities and welfare organizations.
In this fight against unemployment, there are many aspects we cannot readily control; but public works may be resorted to. I may add that the people of this country expect us to take action without delay.
The government has taken the necessary steps to solve the unemployment problem, and the next months should prove that the government forecasts, based on unquestionable statistics, have become facts.

He made it quite clear to the New Zealand embassy in Ottawa, I understand, that there is not much room for more New Zealand cheese in this country at the present time. Strangely enough, however, while the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests to industry what they should do, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture suggests to county councils what they should not do. I would like to quote from an article which appeared in the London Free Press on March 11.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I ask the hon. member what is the relationship between statements made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture and statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with respect to cheese, and the present debate on unemployment? I know the hon. member will want to speak about unemployment on farms and its relationship to unemployment in the cities, but I do not see the relationship of unemployment to the alleged contradictory statements with respect to cheese.

I am sure if I am given a chance to explain you will understand why I made reference to the two statements, because their content does relate to unemployment in this country and I say that advisedly. The importation of New Zealand cheese has a great deal to do with the unemployment situation in Canada. However, having stated that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture seems to want to advise county councils on what they should not do, I wish to quote from an article which appeared in the London Free Press under the dateline of Hensall, March 10. This is what the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture is purported to have said:
"Canada is an exporting country," he said, "and we'll find ourselves in serious difficulties if foreign markets, through reprisals, were shut off to us."
A little further in the article he goes on to say this:
"I don't like to see county councils and other organizations asking the federal government to shut off imports. I don't believe restrictions are the answers to our problems."
Then a little bit further on again we find this:
. . . Mr. McCubbin said, "importation of New Zealand cheese this year is similar to that of the last five years."
"About 2,250,000 pounds of New Zealand cheese has been imported this year for use in process cheese products."
Mr. Speaker, that statement is not correct.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I still do not see the relationship of this analysis of statements made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture to the unemployment situation. I would ask the hon. member to go into the question of unemployment as soon as he can.

I am just pointing out that there are over one million people employed in connection with the dairy industry in this country. Anything that reduces the income of those dairy farmers is bound to cause unemployment. In 1953 there were no importations of New Zealand cheese, and last year there was importation to a total amount of 540 pounds. If that is the same amount over the last five years, I cannot understand it.
Good wages plus cheap food do not equal full employment. Even though the government does not realize that fact, most labour unions do; and it has been mentioned in many of their briefs during the last couple of years. If the farmer's cash income is at a reasonable level, he will buy. Of necessity, in order to protect himself or to assure his future income, he must keep up to date in order to keep his costs down. With costs remaining high and with the farm income or farm prices going down, his only possible answer is to produce more at a smaller unit cost, if possible. A small percentage of overproduction often results in just enough surplus over domestic consumption to seriously depress the price if that small surplus is not readily disposed of in the export market.
That is what I referred to Mr. Speaker, when I was talking about the importation of cheese, and how a small surplus of any commodity can depress the domestic market and in that way reduce the farmers' purchasing power. There can be no doubt about that fact. It has been proved beyond a doubt during the last three years, because the farmers' purchasing power or the net

farm income has gone down over 30 per cent in that time. We wonder why it has gone down.
I might say here that the Ontario cheese producers were doing a magnificent job in marketing their own cheese, looking after their own surplus and collecting from their own producers. Then what did this government do? They cut the feet out from under them by importing cheap cheese from another country. Yet the parliamentary assistant to the minister thinks it is all right to keep on doing that. He implies that it is perfectly all right. He says that county councils should not send in these resolutions requesting the government to restrict the imports of cheese.
For instance, the poultry producers were in trouble last year. Prices were greatly reduced. Their purchasing power was down. They therefore could not buy the things they ordinarily would buy to keep factories in production and keep the wheels of industry turning. I wonder why. Here are some figures that might tell us why. In 1953 a total of 311,769 dozen eggs were imported into this country. In 1954, up until November 30, 472,404 dozen eggs were imported. Those figures are for eggs in the shell. Then we come to egg yolk. These figures are in pounds. In 1953 there were imported 64,997 pounds or almost 65,000 pounds. In 1954 that figure jumped to 150,246 pounds. Then again-

To go on with the egg business, Mr. Speaker, I should like to give these further figures. As to egg yolks in the dried state, 413,037 pounds were imported in 1953 and 453,012 pounds in 1954. Then we come to meats. I am just pointing out these figures because this government does not seem to appreciate the fact that farmers want and need a good market in order to purchase manufactured goods so as to keep the wheels of industry turning and people employed.
In 1954, from January 1 to November 30, a total of 3,034,181 pounds of fresh beef and veal were imported into this country. Then here is a figure to which I should like to direct attention. The price of pork has been going down steadily practically all this year. Yet 1,312,162 pounds of fresh pork were imported into the country in 1954 in order to further depress the price of pork to the farmer. As to fresh lamb and mutton, importations in 1954 were 7,207,902 pounds; chickens and fowl, 2,600,250 pounds; turkeys, 3,719,749 pounds. I might say that was only until November 30. I understand that the figure for the total importation of turkeys last year was away up over the 5 million pound mark. Therefore quite a few must have been imported in the month of December.
What about exports?
He is not interested in exports.

Cheaper consumer foods are of little value to a person who is unemployed, especially when that lower price has actually caused him to be in that position. Many cases could be cited of people who are unemployed because of cheap imports into this country. The average farmer spends four to five times as much on manufactured goods as does the average urban dweller.
Are you saying your farmers are very well oil?

I am making that statement. If you want to make a speech you will have plenty of chance.

I was hoping you would be accurate.

If the hon. member wishes to ask me a question I shall be glad to answer it. I am saying that the average farmer spends four or five times as much on manufactured goods as the average urban dweller. That will go to show just how important the farmer is as a consumer of manufactured goods, and how little his income would have to be reduced before it would be felt by industry and retailers alike. Farmers buy the same household goods. They buy practically the same clothes. They buy almost the same food and on top of that they buy all the implements of their trade, machinery, tools, feed and fertilizer. Why is it that in my own city of Brantford the implement manufacturing companies have been so badly off in the last two years? Unemployment has probably been greater in that industry than in any other in the country.
Evidently you want a tariff imposed.
I cannot hear the hon. member.
It becomes evident that you want a tariff put on. You want to protect the manufacturers.

The hon. member has never heard me ask for a tariff on farm implements, and he never will. I do not know whether he is having a pipe dream but I wish he would not try to put words in my mouth. The fact is there is a terrific unemployment situation in the farm implement manufacturing industry. There is just one answer to that. The farmer's purchasing power is down, his income is greatly reduced, and he is getting his old equipment fixed instead of buying new machines. You can see that all over the country in the machine repair shops. You can see many implements being repaired which farmers ordinarily would be turning in on new ones.
Any reduction in the farmer's purchasing power is bound to be felt by industry and retailers. Hence a large percentage of the present unemployment can be traced directly to reduced purchasing by farmers. There never has been a year in the history of this country as far back as the statistics go when an hour's wages would buy so much food. I repeat; there never has been a year in the history of the country when an hour's wages would buy so much food. Does that lead one to believe that the farmer's purchasing power is high compared with other years, or does it give a fairly good reason for the present level of unemployment?

I wish to refer to only three or four figures. In 1913 the retail food costs index was 68, the hourly wage rates index was 54 and the ratio of wages to food costs was 79. In 1932 the retail food costs index was 62, the lowest figure in the table, hourly wage rates stood at 93 and the ratio of wages to food costs was 149. The figures in the table only go as far as 1948. I have here the figures for 1954. In December, 1954, the retail food costs figure was 172, the hourly wage rates figure was 291 and the figure for the ratio of wages to food costs was 169.
Most people would think that during the 1930's food costs in comparison to wages were rather low. The 1913 figure of 68 for retail food costs had risen by 1954 by not quite three times. Hourly wage rates have increased by better than five times. The ratio between wages and food costs has risen from 79 to 169, an all-time high in the history of these figures. With such a ratio between wages and retail food costs cheap food plus high taxation is bound to equal high unemployment. The government has never considered that high taxation plays any part in the cost of living. Rather than saying we have priced ourselves out of world markets, it seems to me we would be just as correct to say that we have taxed ourselves out of world markets.
I should like to make three suggestions to-the government which I believe would go a long way toward solving our unemployment problem. First, I suggest that the farmers should be assured of reasonable prices for their products. Second, taxation should be reduced and, third, there should be strict administration of the anti-dumping regulations.

Of all
the speeches that have been delivered up to the present time today, Mr. Speaker, I believe that delivered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat is the only one that offered anything positive in relation to the problem of unemployment. It has been rather disheartening to listen to the debate this afternoon. Anyone endeavouring to gather any concrete ideas as to how to attack our problem would surely find his time utterly wasted, because so many of the speeches have completely cancelled themselves; out. For example, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) suggested that we increase expenditures and cut taxation, but he gave no means whereby we could obtain any supplement to the revenues we are now receiving. He left us more or less in uncertainty.
Since this debate began so much of thetalk has been of that nature that I hope-

to be able to follow a line that may at least give some hint as to what might be done. I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat that, in the main, it is far better for us to use our own production in our own country rather than import goods from another country and thereby export employment to that country. Several hon. members have made remarks tending in that direction. I should like to attack the question from the standpoint of increasing the purchasing power in the hands of the people.
That's the ticket.

If hon. members do want
to solve the unemployment problem I suggest they listen. They have no ideas themselves. They are just as empty as an empty barrel. They are just full of a lot of silly babble when somebody else begins to talk. Now, there is something to which it is worth while listening. The Liberals have nothing to which it is worth while listening. The only thing in the world the Liberals have been able to do in the way of providing employment in this country is go to war.
We did not go to war.
Certainly you went to war.
We did not cause the war.

I did not say you did,
but that was the only thing that brought us out of the depression in 1939; and the only thing that saved us from a depression in 1949 was the preparation for the Korean war and participation in that war. Anyone with any sense of reality knows that. Having that in mind, let us face the facts as they are without a lot of silly babble such as you will And in pool rooms, restaurants and all sorts of idle places. Let us not have anything of that kind in the House of Commons where we are supposed to be responsible people.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a number of questions. I expected he would be here tonight, but the fact he is not here will not prevent me from asking the questions. Probably the Prime Minister will require the assistance of the best brains in his party in order to answer these questions. I have been very sympathetic with the Prime Minister ever since this debate began. I do not think I have ever seen a man so full of regrets, chagrin, sorrow and dejection as the Prime Minister has been while sitting here wondering in his own mind whatever could be done about the unemployment problem. Two years ago he came before the Canadian people full of confidence, representing himself as a man

who could take them through the difficulties ahead. He used ways and means whereby he persuaded them to elect him to office. He came out and asked for the position. He took the responsibility, and now he simply cannot discharge it by any means which any of the men in his party are able to suggest to him, or, I venture to say, anyone in the Conservative party.
The C.C.F. does offer something a little different, but the Conservatives do not offer anything different. I listened this afternoon to the fine talk by the hon. member for Prince Albert. If a person had stepped in at any time during his talk and asked him what he would do about this problem he woudl have gone up in smoke, because he as nothing to offer.
Is that why you get along so well with the Conservatives?

Well now, that was a brilliant question; it is one of those things that indicate profundity of comprehension and erudition behind it.
The first question I should like to ask the Prime Minister is, is it in the Prime Mim ister's opinion financially possible in Canada to do a thing which in Canada is physically possible? With that question answered he will be on his way to a possible solution to the country's problems. There is no question but that there are plenty of resources in Canada and plenty of demand for goods in Canada to provide employment for all the people; that has been proven. It is physically possible to provide employment for Canadians. Is there any reason why it cannot be made financially possible?
Old age pensions.

There is another lot of brilliant foolishness, just cheapskate nonsense. That is the size of the hon. member who spoke. He has no ideas of his own, yet he is always making fun of anyone who offers a possible solution to the difficulties. Let the hon. member take that home and sleep on it, and come back with an answer tomorrow.
When the Prime Minister gets an answer to that first question I asked he will be on his way. If it is not physically possible to employ the people of Canada, then we might just as well attack the problem from that angle. If it is physically possible, then our problem is to make what is physically possible financially possible. We want an answer from the Prime Minister to that question: Does the Prime Minister believe that what is physically possible can be made financially possible; yes or no?

We pretty well agreed that during world war II what was physically possible could be made financially possible. I believe the government agreed that such was the case, and undertook to make what was physically possible financially possible.
Following that, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a second question. By what means can what is physically possible be made financially possible? Now, get the answer to that. We can get foolishness down on the street, but what is the answer?
Oh, oh.

Yes, another empty head, full of sound and fury signifying nothing. It is amazing, Mr. Speaker, how many people in this house do not want to solve the unemployment problem in Canada. They are not interested in solving it. All they are interested in is making some silly remarks which they think will get into Hansard and delude the voters. They do not want to solve the unemployment problem. If they did, they would at least listen to something that might offer a solution.
I asked the Prime Minister, by what means can what is physically possible be made financially possible? For example how in world war II did we make what was physically possible financially possible in the war effort?
The third question I want to ask the Prime Minister is this. Does the Prime Minister agree that Canada was able to rather adequately employ all her people during world war II? The answer to that would have to be yes, because we did. The fourth question is, by what means did Canada render financially possible what was physically possible during world war II? By the time we get these four questions answered we should have some ideas with which to go to work to solve the problem before us, as responsible members of the Canadian parliament should be expected to be able to do in this year 1955.
Will the Prime Minister agree that Canada created much of the money with which she rendered financially possible what she achieved during world war II? I ask that of all those brilliant ones who have so much to say, and who had better not talk so much but should do a little thinking. Did Canada create money with which to make what was physically possible in world war II financially possible? I am not sure the Prime Minister will know that. I wish he were here so he could answer it. But just so he can be guided, and several of the bright boys over across the way may be guided also, let me

read something to them from A. F. W. Plumptre which appeared in the Financial Post of October 15, 1940, right after we got into the war. He had this to say:
There are some general matters of theory which must be kept in mind in preparing for the next war loan. It must be remembered, primarily and seemingly paradoxically, that the government's object is not to get money but merely to reduce the public's spending.
The government can always "get money" because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even to taxation, create the required funds. This- it can easily do nowadays through the leadership of the central bank and the co-operation of the chartered banks. In this way $200 million were created in this fashion last autumn.
That was right after Canada entered into world war II. In Canada we created $200 million. All our babblers about funny money can just take that away and think about it.
Will the hon. member not say that almost immediately following the time this $200 million was created prices began to rise? In effect it did have an inflationary tendency.
Well, that is an intelligent question.
One mark for you.

There is a possibility that prices would begin to rise for several reasons. In the first place, Canada was enlisting men and drafting them into the war, and was hiring men in great numbers to go into the munitions plants. All those men were producers or potential producers of goods and services.
Will the hon. member-

Let me do the talking. You can ask all the questions you wish, but for goodness' sake be quiet as I talk and I will keep quiet when you talk. Those facts have to be borne in mind. The hon. member does not question that, does he?
In addition to that we began putting money into the economy where, because of unemployment that had gone on for practically ten years, the country's production effort was at a low ebb. We began taking up great quantities of goods that were in the country to use in the war effort. For example, we began feeding our men as the poor creatures had not been fed for ten years, and we began clothing them instead of allowing them to travel about in rags. We began sheltering them instead of letting them ride on freight cars and camp in the woods. We began immediately to use goods and thereby took them off the market, which tended to create a scarcity of goods.

It was not because the money was going into circulation. It was because of the scarcity of production and production capacity which had been brought on immediately by the war effort. If the goods supply had been kept up that $200 million would not have caused any rise to speak of in prices.
In further answer to my hon. friend's question, I point out that there was not any appreciable rise in prices until 1941, because the wartime prices and trade board was not set up until about that time, which indicates that the $200 million had not caused very much difficulty. To that intelligent question I believe my hon. friend has had an intelligent answer, which he will agree is correct.
I do not agree.

Well, I do not think you would agree to anything that would mean anything at all. I do not know whether you have the apperceiving mass to grasp it. But the important thing is that, regardless of what the effect was, Mr. Plumptre points out that $200 million was created and it was not funny money, not by any means. It was created by the banking institutions in Canada. Is there any conceivable reason why in an emergency such as unemployment the same device cannot be used to solve unemployment problems? I invite Liberals, Conservatives and C.C.F.'ers to concentrate their attention on that question and answer it with the intelligence that befits members of this house; but do not tell us any more that money cannot be created or that money that is created is funny.
